```{python}
#| include: false
# Headline corpus quantities used in the front matter, computed once from the
# analysis universe (S&P 500 at 2021-01-01; the DuckDB manifest views are
# already restricted to it, `paragraphs` is joined back through PANEL_DOCS).
from pathlib import Path
import duckdb
import pandas as pd

_db = Path("../duckdb/thesis.duckdb")
if not _db.exists():
    _db = Path("duckdb/thesis.duckdb")
_db = _db.resolve()
_repo_root = _db.parent.parent

# Persistent connection and search path configuration (views resolve relative to repo root)
_shared_duckdb_conn = duckdb.connect(str(_db), read_only=True)
_shared_duckdb_conn.execute(f"SET file_search_path = '.., {_repo_root}';")
_shared_duckdb_conn.execute("SET enable_progress_bar = false;")

class _DuckDBProxy:
    def __init__(self, conn):
        self._conn = conn
    def close(self):
        pass
    def __getattr__(self, name):
        return getattr(self._conn, name)

_db_proxy = _DuckDBProxy(_shared_duckdb_conn)

con = _db_proxy

def get_db():
    return _db_proxy

# Intercept duckdb.connect so all subsequent cells transparently reuse the shared connection
_orig_duckdb_connect = duckdb.connect
duckdb.connect = lambda *args, **kwargs: _db_proxy

# In-memory Parquet cache to avoid redundant disk I/O and decompression across cells
_orig_read_parquet = pd.read_parquet
_parquet_cache = {}

def _p(name):
    p = Path(f"../data/processed/clusters/{name}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(f"data/processed/clusters/{name}")

def _cached_read_parquet(path, *args, **kwargs):
    try:
        resolved_path = str(Path(path).resolve())
    except Exception:
        return _orig_read_parquet(path, *args, **kwargs)
    cols = kwargs.get("columns", None)
    if not args and (set(kwargs.keys()) <= {"columns"}):
        if resolved_path not in _parquet_cache:
            _parquet_cache[resolved_path] = _orig_read_parquet(resolved_path)
        cached_df = _parquet_cache[resolved_path]
        if cols is not None:
            return cached_df[list(cols)].copy()
        return cached_df.copy()
    return _orig_read_parquet(path, *args, **kwargs)

pd.read_parquet = _cached_read_parquet

PANEL_DOCS = ("accession_number IN ("
              "SELECT accession_number FROM filing_manifest WHERE country_code = 'us' AND accession_number IS NOT NULL "
              "UNION ALL SELECT document_id FROM filing_manifest WHERE country_code = 'us' AND document_id IS NOT NULL "
              "UNION ALL SELECT accession_number FROM filing_manifest_10q WHERE country_code = 'us')")

_c = con
hd_n_docs, hd_n_paragraphs = _c.execute(
    f"SELECT count(DISTINCT accession_number), count(*) FROM paragraphs WHERE country_code = 'us' "
    f"AND form IN ('10-K', '10-Q', '20-F', 'DEF 14A', '8-K', 'Earnings call') AND {PANEL_DOCS}").fetchone()
hd_n_universe = _c.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM firm_universe WHERE country_code = 'us'").fetchone()[0]
_ap = _p("firm_activities.parquet")
_a = pd.read_parquet(_ap, columns=["ticker", "text_hash", "activity_id"]).drop_duplicates()
hd_n_activities = len(_a)
hd_n_activity_firms = int(_a["ticker"].nunique())
hd_paragraphs_m = f"{hd_n_paragraphs / 1e6:.1f}"

# Headline results quoted in the front matter and conclusions, read from the
# same artifacts the empirical chapters compute them from.
import json
_cl = _ap.parent
_m = pd.read_parquet(_cl / "firm_year_master_v2.parquet")
_yr = _m.groupby("year").agg(any_ai=("any_ai", "mean"), frames=("frames_per_1k", "mean"))
hd_share = {int(y): float(v * 100) for y, v in _yr["any_ai"].items()}
hd_frames = {int(y): float(v) for y, v in _yr["frames"].items()}
hd_frames_ratio = hd_frames[2025] / hd_frames[2021]
hd_frames_ratio_26 = hd_frames[2026] / hd_frames[2021]

# Same-window seasonal adjustment for the partial 2026 year: the change in a
# measure between the 2025 window that ends on the same calendar day as the
# 2026 cut-off and the full 2025 year is applied to the 2026 year-to-date value.
_dp = pd.read_parquet(_cl / "document_panel.parquet")
_dp = _dp[_dp["form"].isin(["10-K", "10-Q", "DEF 14A", "8-K"])].copy()
_dp["year"] = _dp["fecha"].dt.year
_dp["md"] = _dp["fecha"].dt.month * 100 + _dp["fecha"].dt.day
hd_cutoff = _dp.loc[_dp["year"] == 2026, "fecha"].max()
hd_cutoff_md = int(hd_cutoff.month * 100 + hd_cutoff.day)
hd_cutoff_str = hd_cutoff.strftime("%-d %B")

def _fy_measures(sub):
    g = sub.groupby("ticker").agg(w=("n_words", "sum"), fr=("n_frames", "sum"))
    return float((1000 * g["fr"] / g["w"]).mean()), float((g["fr"] > 0).mean() * 100)

_full25 = _fy_measures(_dp[_dp["year"] == 2025])
_win25 = _fy_measures(_dp[(_dp["year"] == 2025) & (_dp["md"] <= hd_cutoff_md)])
_ytd26 = _fy_measures(_dp[(_dp["year"] == 2026) & (_dp["md"] <= hd_cutoff_md)])
hd_int_factor = _full25[0] / _win25[0]
hd_share_factor = _full25[1] / _win25[1]
hd_int_est_2026 = _ytd26[0] * hd_int_factor
hd_share_est_2026 = min(_ytd26[1] * hd_share_factor, 100.0)
hd_int_ratio_est = hd_int_est_2026 / hd_frames[2021]
# Activity volumes: same-window factor on the activity count itself.
_ad = pd.read_parquet(_ap, columns=["accession_number", "text_hash", "activity_id"]).drop_duplicates()
_ad = _ad.merge(pd.read_parquet(_cl / "document_panel.parquet", columns=["accession_number", "fecha"]), on="accession_number", how="inner")
_ad["year"] = _ad["fecha"].dt.year
_ad["md"] = _ad["fecha"].dt.month * 100 + _ad["fecha"].dt.day
hd_act_factor = float(((_ad["year"] == 2025).sum()) / ((_ad["year"] == 2025) & (_ad["md"] <= hd_cutoff_md)).sum())
_c = get_db()
_tenk = _c.execute(f"""
    SELECT extract(year FROM fm.filing_date)::INT AS y,
           count(DISTINCT p.accession_number) AS docs,
           count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN f.accession_number IS NOT NULL THEN p.accession_number END) AS docs_ai
    FROM (SELECT DISTINCT accession_number FROM paragraphs WHERE country_code = 'us' AND form = '10-K' AND {PANEL_DOCS}) p
    JOIN filing_manifest fm ON fm.accession_number = p.accession_number AND fm.country_code = 'us'
    LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT accession_number FROM gold_ai_frames WHERE country_code = 'us' AND has_frame AND form = '10-K') f
           ON f.accession_number = p.accession_number
    GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
""").df()
hd_tenk_share = {int(r.y): float(r.docs_ai / r.docs * 100) for r in _tenk.itertuples()}
_gapw = json.loads((_cl / "channel_gap_words_robustness.json").read_text())
hd_promo_ratio = _gapw["promo_per_1k_words"]["ratio"]
hd_quant_ratio = _gapw["quant_per_1k_words"]["ratio"]
_sm = json.loads((_cl / "strategy_dimensions_manifest.json").read_text())
hd_corr = _sm["correlation_matrix"]
hd_stab = {int(k): v for k, v in _sm["stability_by_k"].items()}
hd_stab3 = dict(zip(_sm["cluster_sizes"].keys(), hd_stab[3])) if len(_sm["cluster_sizes"]) == 3 else {}
hd_pca_ev = [x * 100 for x in _sm["pca_diagnostic"]["explained_variance_ratio"]]
_var = _sm["activity_volume_regression"]
hd_vs_ratio = _var["volume_adjusted"]["Vocal Substantives"]["ratio"]
hd_gl_ratio = _var["volume_adjusted"]["Governance-Led Disclosers"]["ratio"]
hd_vol_r2 = _var["r2_adjusted"]
_wv = json.loads((_cl / "washing_score_validation.json").read_text())
hd_w_rho = _wv["persistence"]["spearman"]
_apj = json.loads((_cl / "activity_profiles.json").read_text())
hd_quant_pooled = _apj["top_behaviours"]["quantified_outcome"]
hd_quant_filings = _apj["top_behaviours_filings_only"]["quantified_outcome"]
hd_obj_unspec_firms = _apj["object_families"]["AI, unspecified object"]["pct_firms"]
hd_src_unspec = _apj["distributions"]["source"]["unspecified"]
_inc = json.loads((_cl / "incremental_signal.json").read_text())["outcomes"]["beta"]
hd_inc_n = int(_inc["n_washing"])
hd_inc_r2_base = _inc["r2_M2AB_washing_sample"]
hd_inc_r2_w = _inc["r2_M4"]
hd_inc_dr2 = _inc["delta_r2_washing"]
hd_inc_F = _inc["wald_washing"]["F"]
hd_inc_p = _inc["wald_washing"]["p"]
_cg = json.loads((_cl / "activity_grounding.json").read_text())["channel_gap"]["pooled"]
hd_gap_quant_pp = _cg["quantified_outcome"]["gap_pp"]
hd_gap_named_pp = _cg["named_product_or_process"]["gap_pp"]
```

# Executive Summary {.unnumbered}

After ChatGPT launch in late 2022, almost every S&P 500 firm began discussing AI, making mentions alone uninformative. This thesis separates AI rhetoric from disclosed activity, its grounding, and the gap between them. Across `{python} hd_paragraphs_m` million filing and earnings-call paragraphs, we identify `{python} f"{hd_n_activities:,}"` AI activities across `{python} hd_n_activity_firms` firms.

Corporate AI is mainly applied AI: products, workflows, service, and operations—not foundation technology. Firms follow three disclosure strategies: Vocal Substantives pair frequent discussion with broad, mature activity portfolios; Governance-Led and Defensive Disclosers rely more on oversight or risk language while disclosing less activity. The generative-AI boom increased activity counts, but not their grounding; external tools remain concentrated among U.S. providers.

Credibility differs sharply by venue. Earnings calls contain `{python} round(hd_promo_ratio)`× more promotional and `{python} round(hd_quant_ratio)`× more quantified claims per thousand words than filings, yet quantified outcomes are `{python} f"{hd_gap_quant_pp:.0f}"` percentage points less common in filings for the same firm-year activities. The narrative reaches the binding venue; much of the evidence does not. AI rhetoric—but not disclosed substance or the rhetoric–substance gap—relates to later systematic risk; this is non-causal evidence.

The resulting AI Disclosure Credibility Framework tracks intensity, posture, activity, grounding, substance, decoupling, and consistency across venues. For issuers: move evidence, not adjectives, into the 10-K. For investors: treat a large gap as a due-diligence signal, not a verdict.

# Introduction

## Problem and practical relevance

Following the commercial debut of ChatGPT, artificial intelligence shifted from a specialized technical domain into an omnipresent subject of corporate disclosure [@anantharaman2026, pp. 1--2]. In the U.S. large-cap universe, the proportion of S&P 500 firms making at least one AI-related disclosure in their SEC filings surged from `{python} f"{hd_share[2021]:.0f}"`% in 2021 to `{python} f"{hd_share[2025]:.0f}"`% in 2025, reaching an estimated `{python} f"{hd_share_est_2026:.0f}"`% by the close of 2026. Narrative intensity per thousand words expanded an estimated `{python} f"{hd_int_ratio_est:.0f}"`-fold over the same five-year window.

When corporate discussion becomes near-universal, the mere presence of AI terminology ceases to separate meaningful operational execution from strategic positioning. This creates distinct informational challenges across three primary stakeholder groups:

- **Institutional investors and financial analysts** need to distinguish firms deploying production-grade AI systems from those issuing speculative promotional claims, as operational adoption carries direct valuation and productivity implications [@basnet2025, pp. 1--2; @song2026, pp. 1--2].
- **Corporate managers and boards** face the delicate balance of communicating material technological initiatives to capital markets without generating unachievable expectations or incurring legal liability.
- **Securities regulators** increasingly scrutinize whether public corporate disclosures reflect genuine organizational capabilities or constitute deceptive "AI washing" [@gensler2023, pp. 4--5; @sec2024pressrelease, pp. 1--2]. Recent SEC staff comment letters demonstrate that discrepancies between informal promotional venues and binding statutory filings can directly prompt formal enforcement inquiries [@welltower2025letter, p. 1].

Conventional computational linguistics in finance, based primarily on keyword frequencies or bag-of-words dictionaries [@loughran2011, p. 36], cannot resolve this friction. Such methods treat standard boilerplate risk disclaimers identically to granular, verifiable statements regarding production deployments, capital commitments, or commercial partners. Evaluating corporate credibility requires an empirical approach that measures not only *how much* firms discuss AI, but *how* they frame it, *what* specific operational activities they disclose, and *how concretely* those disclosures are grounded.

## Main research question

Motivated by these empirical and practical tensions, this study addresses the following overarching research question:

> **To what extent does distinguishing disclosure intensity, communication posture, and disclosed operational substance identify meaningful economic differences across firms, and support a credible assessment of corporate AI claims?**

## Objectives and contributions

The primary objective of this thesis is to develop an open, multi-stage measurement framework that audits corporate AI communication across `{python} f"{hd_n_docs:,}"` statutory SEC filings and earnings-call transcripts, and to evaluate the economic credibility of those claims across textual evidence, disclosure channels, regulatory enforcement, and capital markets.

In addressing this objective, the thesis makes three main contributions:

1. **A multi-dimensional measurement architecture.** Moving beyond keyword frequencies and opaque sentiment scores, the study establishes an end-to-end pipeline combining supervised gradient boosting with zero-shot large language model extraction. It measures corporate AI communication across five observable dimensions: narrative intensity, communication posture, operational AI activities, verification grounding, and observable decoupling.
2. **Multi-angle empirical tests linking theory to corporate evidence.** Rather than analyzing corporate discourse in isolation, the study tests theoretical mechanisms across four analytical settings: market-wide diffusion and communication archetypes (Chapter 3), operational activity mapping and economic coherence (Chapter 4), cross-venue credibility gaps and SEC comment-letter scrutiny (Chapter 5), and capital-market pricing of systematic risk (Chapter 6).
3. **A practical credibility framework for diligence and strategy.** Translating measurement into decision-making tools, the thesis operationalizes a credibility framework (Chapter 7) featuring portfolio screening matrices and compliance benchmarks that help investors and corporate issuers separate substantive AI integration from promotional cheap talk.

## Theoretical foundations and state of the art

### What the literature knows and prior empirical evidence

This thesis connects with the literature applying computational linguistics and textual analysis to corporate disclosure and finance [@li2008, pp. 1--3; @loughran2011, pp. 35--36; @gentzkow2019, pp. 1--2; @hoberg2016; @hassan2019]. Recent empirical studies document the sharp acceleration of corporate AI discussion following the generative AI shock [@anantharaman2026, pp. 1--2]. In response, researchers have sought to classify AI language into actionable versus speculative statements [@basnet2025, pp. 1--2], measure planned versus implemented AI using patent records and hiring data [@song2026, pp. 1--2; @babina2024], and estimate firm-level exposure from occupational employment structures [@eisfeldt2023, p. 9].

At the same time, heightened capital-market enthusiasm has focused academic and regulatory attention on "AI washing"—corporate claims that lack genuine operational substance [@gensler2023, pp. 4--5; @sec2024pressrelease, pp. 1--2]. This inquiry draws from research on greenwashing and symbolic management [@delmas2011, pp. 64--68; @lyon2015, pp. 1--3; @marquis2016, pp. 483--85], and from evidence that managers strategically manipulate qualitative disclosure tone independently of financial fundamentals [@huang2014] and inflate speculative disclosures during emerging technology booms [@cheng2019].

### Theoretical concepts and mechanisms

Four theoretical perspectives motivate the empirical architecture of this thesis:

* **Signalling and cheap talk.** Corporate claims achieve credibility only when containing verifiable details that are costly to fake or straightforward to audit [@spence1973, pp. 363--64; @crawford1982, pp. 1431--32; @dye1985, pp. 123--24]. When disclosure carries low verification costs and minimal legal liability, economic theory predicts ungrounded promotional posturing ("cheap talk"). Assessing credibility therefore requires separating generic language from hard-to-fake operational evidence, including named software systems, deployment stages, quantified metrics, and identified technology partners [@rogers2011, pp. 2155--56].
* **Institutional legitimacy and diffusion.** Under high technological uncertainty, organizations face normative and mimetic pressures to adopt ceremonial symbols and fashionable narratives [@meyer1977, pp. 340--41; @dimaggio1983, pp. 147--48; @suchman1995, pp. 571--74]. Stakeholders expect an AI narrative regardless of whether internal workflows have materially changed. This mechanism explains why AI disclosure diffuses rapidly across entire industries and why disclosure postures coalesce into discrete, recurrent archetypes [@hennig2007, pp. 1--2].
* **Decoupling and symbolic management.** Organizational sociology distinguishes formal symbolic structures from actual operational practices [@meyer1977, pp. 340--41; @westphal1994, pp. 367--69; @crilly2012, pp. 1429--31; @bromley2012]. Because enterprise AI adoption lacks a centralized, audited reporting registry, this study examines observable decoupling: the empirical divergence between a firm's high-level narrative intensity and its disclosed, grounded operational activities.
* **Regulatory enforcement and credibility boundaries.** Public enforcement agencies alter the cost structure of corporate disclosure [@gensler2023, pp. 4--5; @sec2024pressrelease]. Differences in legal liability across communication channels—such as formal statutory SEC filings versus voluntary earnings calls [@matsumoto2011, pp. 1383--84; @frankel1999, pp. 133--34]—provide boundary conditions to test whether external scrutiny constrains cheap talk and compels operational grounding.

### Literature gaps: what remains unknown

Prior research has established that corporate AI disclosures have expanded dramatically and that managers adjust narrative tone strategically around technological transitions. However, critical empirical gaps remain at the intersection of these literatures:

1. **Granular operational inventory:** We know that firms frequently mention AI, but we do not yet know how to systematically isolate and categorize discrete operational actions from narrative boilerplate at full market scale.
2. **Cross-venue divergence:** We know that voluntary earnings calls involve lower litigation risk than annual Form 10-K filings, but we do not yet know how promotional rhetoric and quantifiable evidence systematically diverge across these venues for the same firm-year.
3. **Internal observable decoupling:** We know that symbolic decoupling occurs when external monitoring is imperfect, but in the absence of external audit data for enterprise AI, the literature lacks a calibrated measure of decoupling based on internal consistency between narrative volume and grounded activity.
4. **Capital market pricing:** We know that markets react to technology narratives, but it remains unexamined whether capital markets price verifiable operational substance or merely respond to sheer disclosure volume.

## Hypotheses and research questions

To address these gaps through our theoretical mechanisms, we formulate a central hypothesis and four guiding research questions:

**Main hypothesis.** Disclosure posture and grounded operational substance carry incremental information about firm operating characteristics and market risk beyond narrative disclosure volume alone.

Four linked research questions guide the empirical chapters:

- **RQ1: Evolution and composition (Chapter 3).** *How has corporate AI disclosure evolved across the market, and what concrete operational activities do firms report?* Derived from institutional diffusion theory, this question evaluates whether market-wide AI adoption reflects ceremonial compliance or genuine operational deployment.
- **RQ2: Strategic heterogeneity and economic coherence (Chapters 3 & 4).** *Which recurring communication archetypes set firms apart, and do their disclosed activities cohere with underlying economic fundamentals?* Derived from configuration theory and signalling, this question tests whether distinct disclosure postures reflect genuine economic endowments rather than random noise.
- **RQ3: Credibility, decoupling, and venue divergence (Chapter 5).** *Where do gaps open between narrative volume and grounded substance, and how do promotional claims shift between informal calls and statutory filings?* Derived from cheap talk, decoupling, and regulatory enforcement, this question tests whether liability differences and SEC comment letters discipline corporate communication.
- **RQ4: Market pricing and information content (Chapter 6).** *Does capital-market pricing reflect grounded operational substance, or do investors respond indiscriminately to narrative volume?* Derived from signalling theory, this question tests whether post-call systematic risk responds to substantive operational signals or cheap talk.

# Methodology

## Data sources and corpus

The U.S. corpus covers 10-K, 10-Q, 20-F, DEF 14A, and 8-K filings for the S&P 500 universe plus earnings-call transcripts from 2021 through early 2026. Document counts and deduplication statistics are dynamically computed from the processed database.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
_u = con.execute("SELECT active_status, count(*) AS n FROM firm_universe WHERE country_code = 'us' GROUP BY 1").df()
uni_frame_total = int(_u["n"].sum())
uni_frame_delisted = int(_u.loc[_u["active_status"] == "delisted", "n"].sum())

_master = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_year_master_v2.parquet"))
uni_n_firms = int(_master["ticker"].nunique())
_yrs = _master.groupby("ticker")["year"].nunique()
bal_n = int((_yrs == 6).sum())
bal_share = (_master[_master["ticker"].isin(_yrs[_yrs == 6].index)]
             .groupby("year").apply(lambda s: (s["n_frames"] > 0).mean() * 100)).to_dict()
uni_n_activity_firms = int(pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_activities.parquet"))["ticker"].nunique())

# Temporal coverage of the partial 2026 year, from the manifests.
_cov = con.execute("""
    SELECT form_type, count(DISTINCT ticker) AS firms, max(filing_date) AS last_date
    FROM (SELECT form_type, ticker, filing_date FROM filing_manifest WHERE country_code = 'us'
          UNION ALL SELECT '10-Q', ticker, filing_date FROM filing_manifest_10q WHERE country_code = 'us')
    WHERE extract(year FROM filing_date) = 2026 GROUP BY 1
""").df().set_index("form_type")
_cov25 = con.execute("SELECT count(DISTINCT ticker) FROM filing_manifest WHERE country_code = 'us' AND form_type = '10-K' AND extract(year FROM filing_date) = 2025").fetchone()[0]
cov_last_date = str(pd.to_datetime(_cov["last_date"].max()).date())
cov_10k_2026 = int(_cov.loc["10-K", "firms"]) if "10-K" in _cov.index else 0
cov_10k_2025 = int(_cov25)
cov_10q_2026 = int(_cov.loc["10-Q", "firms"]) if "10-Q" in _cov.index else 0
cov_calls_2026 = int(_cov.loc["Earnings call transcript", "firms"]) if "Earnings call transcript" in _cov.index else 0
cov_months_2026 = pd.to_datetime(cov_last_date).month
```

**Firm universe and panel construction.** The sample starts from the S&P 500 constituents as of 2021-01-01 (`{python} uni_frame_total` tickers). To avoid survivorship bias, the `{python} uni_frame_delisted` firms subsequently delisted or acquired remain in the panel through their exit dates. Overall, `{python} uni_n_firms` firms have processed narrative records, `{python} uni_n_activity_firms` disclose operational AI activities, and `{python} bal_n` firms form a balanced cohort observed across all six years (2021–2026).

**Temporal coverage and seasonal adjustment.** The panel closes with filings through `{python} cov_last_date`. For partial-year 2026, `{python} cov_10k_2026` firms have filed annual 10-Ks (versus `{python} cov_10k_2025` in full-year 2025), `{python} cov_10q_2026` filed 10-Qs, and `{python} cov_calls_2026` hosted earnings calls. While cross-sectional distributions (archetypes, Decoupling, grounding) are evaluated on observed year-to-date disclosures, annual trend comparisons apply a same-window seasonal adjustment scaling 2026 by the ratio of full-year 2025 to the matching 2025 calendar window (`{python} hd_cutoff_str`).

```{python}
#| echo: false
from IPython.display import Markdown
# Documents of the analysis universe (S&P 500 at 2021-01-01). The manifest
# views are already restricted to that panel; `paragraphs` is a base table
# keyed by accession_number (calls use their document_id), so every corpus
# count joins back to the manifests through this predicate.
PANEL_DOCS = ("accession_number IN ("
              "SELECT accession_number FROM filing_manifest WHERE country_code = 'us' AND accession_number IS NOT NULL "
              "UNION ALL SELECT document_id FROM filing_manifest WHERE country_code = 'us' AND document_id IS NOT NULL "
              "UNION ALL SELECT accession_number FROM filing_manifest_10q WHERE country_code = 'us')")
scope = f"country_code = 'us' AND form IN ('10-K', '10-Q', '20-F', 'DEF 14A', '8-K', 'Earnings call') AND {PANEL_DOCS}"
totals = con.execute(f"""
    SELECT count(DISTINCT accession_number) AS documents,
           count(*) AS paragraphs,
           sum(is_scorable::INT) AS scorable,
           count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN is_scorable THEN text_hash END) AS unique_texts
    FROM paragraphs WHERE {scope}
""").fetchone()
con.close()
```

```{python}
from IPython.display import Markdown

n_docs, n_raw, n_scorable, n_unique = totals[0], totals[1], totals[2], totals[3]
n_prefiltered = con.execute(f"""
    SELECT count(*) FROM (
        SELECT text_hash, is_ai_prefiltered
        FROM read_parquet('data/interim/prefilter_predictions_unique/prefilter_predictions__run=*.parquet', union_by_name=true)
        WHERE country_code = 'us'
        QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY text_hash ORDER BY model_version DESC) = 1
    ) WHERE is_ai_prefiltered
      AND text_hash IN (SELECT text_hash FROM paragraphs WHERE country_code='us' AND is_scorable AND {PANEL_DOCS})
""").fetchone()[0]

con.execute(f"""
    CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP TABLE _us_frames AS
    SELECT form, accession_number, paragraph_index, text_hash, frame_id, subject, ai_type, temporal, specificity, rhetoric
    FROM gold_ai_frames WHERE country_code='us' AND has_frame AND {PANEL_DOCS}
""")
n_framed, n_frames_total, share_firm_subject, n_firm_texts = con.execute("""
    SELECT 
        count(DISTINCT text_hash) AS n_framed,
        count(*) AS n_frames_total,
        avg((subject = 'firm')::INT) * 100 AS share_firm_subject,
        count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN subject = 'firm' THEN text_hash END) AS n_firm_texts
    FROM (SELECT DISTINCT text_hash, frame_id, subject FROM _us_frames)
""").fetchone()
n_activities = hd_n_activities

rows = [
    ("1. Raw Corpus", "Paragraph instances", f"Raw segmentation across {n_docs:,} filings & calls", n_raw, 100.0),
    ("2. Scorable Filter", "Scorable instances", "Length (>3 chars) & alphanumeric content", n_scorable, n_scorable / n_raw * 100),
    ("3. Deduplication", "Unique scorable texts", "BLAKE2b content hash", n_unique, n_unique / n_raw * 100),
    ("4. Machine Learning Gate", "Candidate paragraphs", "Supervised GBDT (classification threshold tau=0.17)", n_prefiltered, n_prefiltered / n_raw * 100),
    ("5. Semantic Frames", "Texts with >=1 frame", "Zero-shot LLM judge (gpt-5.6-luna)", n_framed, n_framed / n_raw * 100),
    ("6. Disclosed AI Activities", "Operational action triples", "Firm-conditioned LLM extraction (pass 2)", n_activities, n_activities / n_raw * 100),
]
table = [[stage, unit, filt, f"{count:,}", f"{share:.2f}%"] for stage, unit, filt, count, share in rows]
Markdown(tabulate(table, headers=["Stage", "Unit of Observation", "Operational Filter", "Retained Volume", "Share of Raw"]))
```

*Notes: High-level overview of the six-stage inference funnel. Granular form-by-form decompositions and model acceptance diagnostics are detailed in Appendix A (@tbl-a1-funnel-full).*

The end-to-end architecture (@fig-pipeline-architecture; @tbl-funnel-summary) transforms raw corporate text into structured analytical metrics through two intermediate representations:

$$\text{Raw text} \longrightarrow \text{AI claims (Frames)} \longrightarrow \text{Disclosed AI activities} \longrightarrow \text{Firm-level measures}$$

## Identifying AI disclosure: cleaning, deduplication, and ML gate

Before model evaluation, scorable paragraphs ($>3$ characters, alphanumeric content) are normalized and hashed using BLAKE2b content signatures. Deduplication ensures that identical regulatory boilerplate and legal disclaimers are scored only once per unique text and mapped back across all containing filings, preventing recycled narrative from distorting downstream measures.

Candidate texts are identified using a supervised Gradient Boosted Decision Tree (GBDT) prefilter [@friedman2001, pp. 1189--95] combining 39 lexical, semantic, structural, and sentence-embedding signals. To ensure minimal information loss ahead of the LLM pass, the classifier is tuned for high recall ($\ge 0.92$, probability classification threshold $\tau = 0.17$). Non-disclosing documents are explicitly recorded as true zeros rather than missing values. Corpus attrition across each screening stage is detailed in @tbl-funnel-summary, with out-of-domain and human validation reported in Appendix A (@tbl-evaluation-datasets).

## From paragraphs to individual AI claims: frame extraction

Candidate texts pass to a zero-shot large language model judge (`openai/gpt-5.6-luna`), selected for extraction fidelity and consistency across foundation model benchmarks (Appendix A). The judge operates as a high-precision gate: it discards roughly `{python} f"{(1 - n_framed / n_prefiltered) * 100:.0f}"`% of prefiltered candidates that contain only stray keywords, macroeconomic commentary, or generic risk disclosures.

For surviving disclosures, the judge extracts zero, one, or several structured claims per text across a standard seven-dimension schema (@tbl-frame-schema). Claims attributing operational actions or exposures to the disclosing firm itself provide the empirical foundation for AI Disclosure Intensity ($D$) and Communication Posture ($P$).


## From claims to concrete AI activities: action, object, and function

When a frame attributes an operational action to the reporting firm (deploying, developing, partnering, investing, hiring, or scaling), it enters a second-pass extraction prompt conditioned on the firm's identity (ticker and legal name) to resolve corporate attribution. The prompt extracts an operational action triple (action, object, function), maturity stage, technology sourcing, beneficiaries, and verification anchors (@tbl-activity-schema).

Across the panel, this extraction identifies `{python} f"{hd_n_activities:,}"` unique operational AI activity records across `{python} hd_n_activity_firms` S&P 500 firms, anchored to exact sentence citations in source documents. These records serve as inputs to Disclosed AI Activity ($A$) and Activity Grounding ($G$).

## From extracted evidence to analytical constructs

The extraction pipeline aggregates semantic frames and operational activity records into six core constructs:

$$\underbrace{\text{Semantic frames}}_{\text{frame extraction}} \Longrightarrow D, P \qquad\qquad \underbrace{\text{AI Activity records}}_{\text{activity extraction}} \Longrightarrow A, G \qquad\qquad (D, A, G) \Longrightarrow S \Longrightarrow W$$

1. **AI Disclosure Intensity ($D$):** Narrative discussion volume, defined as AI semantic frames per 1,000 words of scorable text to normalize for document length:
   $$D_{it} = \frac{\text{AI frames}_{it}}{\text{words}_{it} / 1{,}000}$$
2. **Communication Posture ($P$):** A six-dimensional vector capturing *how* the firm discusses AI: claim realization, risk orientation, governance focus, objective specificity, customer orientation, and promotional tone.
3. **Disclosed AI Activity ($A$):** Count of discrete operational action triples ($n_{\text{activities}}$) across six business domains.
4. **AI Activity Grounding ($G$):** An unweighted verifiability index in $[0, 1]$ reflecting the proportion of five concrete checks met: specific business function, deployed/scaled stage, named product/process, quantified metric, and named technology provider.
5. **Disclosed Substance ($S$):** Grounded operational volume, scaling log activity count by grounding quality:
   $$S_{it} = \log(1 + n_{\text{activities},it}) \times G_{it}$$
6. **Decoupling ($W$):** The signed percentile-rank difference between narrative volume and grounded substance across disclosing firm-years:
   $$W_{it} = \text{rank}(D_{it}) - \text{rank}(S_{it}) \in [-1, 1]$$
   Persistent positive decoupling reflects what is colloquially termed "AI washing."

**Aggregation and measurement robustness.** Document intensities are aggregated to firm-years using the median document rate, preventing distortion from isolated boilerplate exhibits. Operational concept counts are log-transformed, which demonstrates superior test-retest reliability over discourse shares ($\rho = 0.845$ vs. $0.528$). Rates for firms with sparse disclosure are shrunk toward the corpus mean via empirical-Bayes estimation [@efron1973].

## Financial and market variables

Firm-year accounting and market variables are drawn from SEC XBRL filings and daily market return series, aligned to actual fiscal period ends rather than filing dates. Financial metrics apply standardized concept fallback rules (capex 91%, SG&A 81%, net margin 99%, revenue 99% coverage) and a [340, 380]-day interval filter for annual changes.

The baseline covariates comprise market capitalization, R&D-to-sales, gross margin, operating margin, asset turnover, price-to-sales, next-period revenue growth, market beta, and idiosyncratic volatility [@campbell2001; @ang2006]. Because R&D reporting in XBRL has 46% coverage, it is treated as a separate indicator rather than imputing zero for non-reporters. All financial ratios are winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles. Appendix D details estimation windows, delisting treatments, and beta diagnostics.

## Measurement validation

Every automated stage of the extraction pipeline is audited against held-out ground truth, independent multi-model evaluations, and manual human reviews. These benchmarks confirm high classification fidelity across model families (Gemini 3.8 and Qwen 3.7 inter-judge agreement $\kappa = 0.81\text{--}0.87$) and against blind human audits (91.2% precision on prefiltering, 89.1%–95.8% field accuracy on activity extraction). Complete sample constructions, out-of-domain transfer benchmarks, and evaluation metrics are reported in Appendix A (@tbl-evaluation-datasets).

# Corporate AI Disclosure Strategies

## AI becomes ubiquitous

AI went from a niche topic to a standard item of corporate disclosure between 2021 and 2026. The share of S&P 500 firms making at least one AI statement in their SEC filings rose from `{python} f"{hd_share[2021]:.1f}"`% in 2021 to `{python} f"{hd_share[2025]:.1f}"`% in 2025, the last complete year, and reached `{python} f"{hd_share[2026]:.1f}"`% in the 2026 year-to-date sample (@fig-ai-diffusion).

Narrative intensity, AI semantic frames per 1,000 words of corporate text, climbed from `{python} f"{hd_frames[2021]:.3f}"` in 2021 to `{python} f"{hd_frames[2025]:.3f}"` in 2025 (`{python} f"{hd_frames_ratio:.1f}"`-fold), and stands at `{python} f"{hd_frames[2026]:.3f}"` in 2026 year to date.

Year-to-date values are not comparable with full years because the document mix is seasonal: annual reports cluster in the first quarter. We therefore estimate full-year 2026 with a same-window adjustment. In 2025, the change from the window ending on `{python} hd_cutoff_str` to the full year was a factor of `{python} f"{hd_int_factor:.3f}"` for intensity and `{python} f"{hd_share_factor:.3f}"` for participation. Applied to the 2026 year-to-date values, those factors give an estimated `{python} f"{hd_int_est_2026:.3f}"` frames per 1,000 words (`{python} f"{hd_int_ratio_est:.1f}"`-fold since 2021) and `{python} f"{hd_share_est_2026:.1f}"`% participation at the close of 2026.

The sharpest jump comes in the 2023–2024 filing season, when fiscal-year-2023 10-Ks became the first annual reports written after a full year of generative AI commercialization. The share of 10-Ks with any AI content went from `{python} f"{hd_tenk_share[2023]:.0f}"`% to `{python} f"{hd_tenk_share[2024]:.0f}"`% in one season. A balanced cohort of the `{python} bal_n` firms observed every year from 2021 to 2026 follows the same path (`{python} f"{bal_share[2021]:.0f}"`% to `{python} f"{bal_share[2025]:.0f}"`%). This is market-wide adoption, not survivorship or index rebalancing.


Once almost every large firm talks about AI, presence alone says little. At `{python} f"{hd_share[2025]:.1f}"`% participation, *whether* a firm discloses AI no longer separates firms. What separates them is *how* they communicate: the framing, emphasis, risk perception, and specificity that make up their disclosure posture.

## The dimensions of AI disclosure strategy

Six frame-level dimensions describe Communication Posture ($P$). Disclosure intensity $D$ completes the set. @tbl-strategy-dimensions defines each dimension and its managerial meaning. @fig-strategy-dimensions-dist shows their distribution across the S&P 500.

|---|---|---|---|
| **Promotional posture** | Average of promotional tone and strategic-importance framing | $[0, 1]$ | Extent to which AI is communicated as a transformative strategic asset |
| **Hedging posture** | Share of statements framed with cautious or conditional language | $[0, 1]$ | Degree to which AI claims are qualified rather than asserted outright |
| **Risk orientation** | Share of statements containing risk, uncertainty, or dependency concepts | $[0, 1]$ | Degree to which AI is treated as an operational vulnerability or hazard |
| **Governance orientation** | Share of statements containing oversight, ethics, or compliance policies | $[0, 1]$ | Formal institutionalization of model oversight and responsible AI guardrails |
| **Temporal posture** | Share of statements describing realized rather than planned actions | $[0, 1]$ | Operational maturity: active deployment vs. speculative roadmap |
| **AI positioning** | Share of statements framed toward clients and external products | $[0, 1]$ | Commercial orientation: revenue generation vs. internal cost-cutting |
| **Specificity** | Mean of 5 binary grounding flags (process, product, vendor, metric, timeline) | $[0, 1]$ | Falsifiability and informational granularity of corporate statements |
| **Disclosure intensity** | Percentile rank of AI semantic frames per 1,000 narrative words | $[0, 1]$ | Overall volume of narrative communication dedicated to artificial intelligence |

: Operational definitions of the eight AI disclosure strategy dimensions. {#tbl-strategy-dimensions}

The correlation structure of these eight dimensions shows two key properties. The full matrix appears in @tbl-a3-posture-correlation (Appendix C):

1. Governance framing is largely independent of other dimensions. Governance orientation barely correlates with promotional posture ($r =$ `{python} f"{hd_corr['governance_orientation']['promotional_posture']:.2f}"`), risk framing ($r =$ `{python} f"{hd_corr['governance_orientation']['risk_orientation']:.2f}"`), or disclosure intensity ($r =$ `{python} f"{hd_corr['governance_orientation']['disclosure_intensity']:.2f}"`). It forms its own layer. It does not proxy for verbosity or risk aversion.
2. Risk orientation runs against concrete execution. Risk framing correlates negatively with realized temporal posture ($r =$ `{python} f"{hd_corr['risk_orientation']['temporal_posture']:.2f}"`), specificity ($r =$ `{python} f"{hd_corr['risk_orientation']['specificity']:.2f}"`), customer-facing positioning ($r =$ `{python} f"{hd_corr['risk_orientation']['ai_positioning']:.2f}"`), and intensity ($r =$ `{python} f"{hd_corr['risk_orientation']['disclosure_intensity']:.2f}"`). Firms that treat AI mainly as a hazard say less about it. They name fewer concrete tools. They rarely report client-facing deployments.

## Recurrent disclosure archetypes

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd


_arch = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_strategy_dimensions.parquet"))
arch_n_universe = len(_arch)
arch_n_noai = int((_arch["archetype"] == "No AI").sum())
arch_n_fit = arch_n_universe - arch_n_noai
```

We compute the posture dimensions across all `{python} arch_n_universe` firms. Firms with fewer than five AI frames across 2021–2025 SEC filings receive the rule-based label **No AI** ($n =$ `{python} arch_n_noai`). By 2025, nearly nine in ten firms disclose enough AI commentary to exhibit an active posture [@dimaggio1983, pp. 147--48].

For the active firms ($n =$ `{python} arch_n_fit`), disclosure strategies blend distinct communication registers rather than falling into rigid discrete bins. We apply continuous **Archetypal Analysis** [@cutler1994, pp. 338--47] to the eight standardized posture dimensions. Every firm $i$ is represented as a convex combination of $k$ extreme boundary vertices:

$$x_i \approx \sum_{j=1}^k w_{ij} z_j, \quad \text{subject to} \quad \sum_{j=1}^k w_{ij} = 1, \quad w_{ij} \ge 0$$

where $z_j \in \mathbb{R}^7$ are the archetypal coordinate vectors and $w_{ij}$ are the barycentric weights reflecting the firm's posture portfolio.

### Recurrent archetypal profiles and the disclosure simplex

Fitting Archetypal Analysis at $k = 3$ projects every active disclosing firm onto the 2-simplex $\Delta^2$ spanned by three extreme boundary vertices. @fig-archetypal-ternary-simplex maps all `{python} arch_n_fit` disclosing index constituents onto this continuous disclosure simplex, displaying consolidated industry centroids alongside boundary and central exemplars:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-archetypes-glance
#| tbl-cap: "AI corporate disclosure archetypes at a glance. Archetypal disclosure profile reports the standardized coordinate score (SD from the pooled mean of active firms) on the dimensions that define each archetype; stability reports the mean bootstrap Jaccard reproducibility under frame-level resampling."
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown


_g = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_strategy_dimensions.parquet"))
_feats = {"promotional_posture": "promotional", "hedging_posture": "hedging", "risk_orientation": "risk", "governance_orientation": "governance",
          "temporal_posture": "realized", "ai_positioning": "customer-facing", "specificity": "specificity",
          "disclosure_intensity": "intensity"}
_fit = _g[_g["archetype"] != "No AI"]
_n = _g["archetype"].value_counts()
# Stability read live from build_strategy_dimensions.py's own bootstrap output
# (`archetype_stability`, constant within an archetype -- one mean Jaccard
# per cluster, broadcast to its members), not a value typed in here by hand.
_stab = _g.groupby("archetype")["archetype_stability"].first().to_dict()
arch_share = (_n / len(_g) * 100).round(1).to_dict()

# Archetypal profile text generated from the actual fitted z-scores, not
# hand-typed: standardize each of the 8 posture dimensions over the active
# population (same standardization `build_strategy_dimensions.py` clusters
# on), take each archetype's mean z per dimension, and report the
# dimensions that separate it most (|z| >= 0.5), strongest first.
_z = (_fit[list(_feats)] - _fit[list(_feats)].mean()) / _fit[list(_feats)].std(ddof=0)
_z["archetype"] = _fit["archetype"].values
_zmean = _z.groupby("archetype")[list(_feats)].mean()

def _profile_text(archetype: str, threshold: float = 0.5) -> str:
    row = _zmean.loc[archetype].sort_values(key=lambda s: -s.abs())
    high = [(_feats[c], v) for c, v in row.items() if v >= threshold]
    low = [(_feats[c], v) for c, v in row.items() if v <= -threshold]
    parts = []
    if high:
        parts.append("High " + ", ".join(f"{name} ({v:+.2f} SD)" for name, v in high))
    if low:
        parts.append("low " + ", ".join(f"{name} ({v:+.2f} SD)" for name, v in low))
    return "; ".join(parts) if parts else "No dimension separates by >=0.5 SD"

_profiles = {a: _profile_text(a) for a in ["Vocal Substantives", "Governance-Led Disclosers", "Defensive Disclosers"]}

_rows = []
for a in ["Vocal Substantives", "Governance-Led Disclosers", "Defensive Disclosers"]:
    _rows.append([f"**{a}**", int(_n[a]), f"{arch_share[a]:.1f}%", _profiles[a], f"{_stab[a]:.2f}"])
_rows.append(["**No AI**", int(_n["No AI"]), f"{arch_share['No AI']:.1f}%",
              "Fewer than 5 pooled AI frames across 2021–2025 SEC filings (rule-based filter)", f"{_stab['No AI']:.2f}"])
Markdown(tabulate(_rows, headers=["Archetype", "Firms ($n$)", "Share (%)", "Archetypal disclosure profile", "Stability (Jaccard)"]))
```

The three archetypes reflect distinct strategic orientations (@tbl-archetypes-glance):

- **Vocal Substantives:** Commercial execution and product differentiation. Issuers at this pole actively commercialize AI for external clients, pairing promotional forward guidance with verifiable technical claims (naming concrete systems, partner ecosystems, and performance metrics) to establish market credibility.
- **Governance-Led Disclosers:** Institutional oversight and risk containment. Rather than marketing commercial tools, these issuers prioritize supervisory guardrails, emphasizing board committee charters, model-risk auditing protocols, and responsible AI frameworks.
- **Defensive Disclosers:** Passive regulatory compliance. These firms treat AI primarily as an operational hazard, satisfying statutory disclosure mandates by listing boilerplate risks in Item 1A without committing management to operational milestones or concrete deployments.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-representative-firms
#| tbl-cap: "Representative corporations and disclosure registers across AI disclosure archetypes. Prominent constituents are widely recognized S&P 500 members in each cluster; centroid-closest exemplars are the firms nearest to each archetype's mean standardized posture vector; primary SEC disclosure focus summarizes the dominant narrative register in statutory filings."
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown
fu = con.execute("SELECT ticker, company_name, sic, active_status FROM firm_universe WHERE country_code = 'us'").df()
fu_delisted = set(fu.loc[fu["active_status"] == "delisted", "ticker"])
fu["sic2"] = fu["sic"].astype(str).str.zfill(4).str[:2]

df_strat = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_strategy_dimensions.parquet"))
df_sec = df_strat.merge(fu, on="ticker", how="left")

_feat_cols = ["promotional_posture", "hedging_posture", "risk_orientation", "governance_orientation", "temporal_posture",
              "ai_positioning", "specificity", "disclosure_intensity"]
_fit = df_sec[df_sec["archetype"] != "No AI"].copy()
_zz = (_fit[_feat_cols] - _fit[_feat_cols].mean()) / _fit[_feat_cols].std()

def _clean_name(n):
    n = str(n)
    for suf in [", Inc.", " Inc.", " Inc", " Corporation", " Corp.", " Corp", " Company", " Co.", " plc", " PLC", " Holdings", " Ltd."]:
        n = n.replace(suf, "")
    return n.strip()

def _closest(a, k=4):
    idx = _fit.index[_fit["archetype"] == a]
    c = _zz.loc[idx].mean().values
    dist = np.linalg.norm(_zz.loc[idx].values - c, axis=1)
    best = idx[np.argsort(dist)[:k]]
    return ", ".join(f"{_clean_name(_fit.loc[i, 'company_name'])} (`{_fit.loc[i, 'ticker']}`)" for i in best)

prominent = {
```

Individual firms illustrate how the taxonomy distinguishes communication strategies (@tbl-representative-firms). Vocal Substantives concentrate among infrastructure and platform providers that monetize AI directly. Governance-Led Disclosers span heavily regulated institutions that emphasize supervisory guardrails and fiduciary compliance. Defensive Disclosers encompass consumer and industrial firms that treat AI primarily as a competitive exposure or operational dependency.

Two high-profile classifications illustrate the distinction between SEC disclosure posture and commercial reputation:

- **Apple** clusters as Governance-Led: while it deploys proprietary AI across its consumer devices, its statutory SEC filings concentrate AI mentions on board oversight, privacy policies, and responsible-use shareholder proposals, reserving product marketing for consumer keynotes outside EDGAR.
- **Goldman Sachs** clusters as Defensive: over 60% of its AI-bearing text resides in Item 1A risk factors (model risk, cybersecurity, and vendor dependencies), with minimal operational disclosure of the kind Vocal Substantives report in the same filings.

Capital-intensive firms with little digital-transformation discourse, such as Costco, Texas Instruments, O'Reilly Automotive, and NVR, make up the No AI group. It also absorbs firms that left the index through acquisition or delisting before the generative-AI boom: `{python} int(df_sec.loc[df_sec["archetype"] == "No AI", "ticker"].isin(fu_delisted).sum())` of the `{python} int((df_sec["archetype"] == "No AI").sum())` No AI firms are delisted. They never had a post-2023 filing in which to adopt the new vocabulary. Keeping them avoids survivorship bias, but it means "No AI" partly reflects exit timing rather than a deliberate stance.

### Model selection: bootstrap stability and falsification

To determine the number of archetypes $k$, we evaluate reproducibility across $k \in \{2, 3, 4, 5\}$ under two non-parametric bootstrap regimes with 200 independent replicates (@fig-archetype-stability): (1) frame-level resampling within firms (evaluating measurement error), and (2) firm-level resampling (evaluating sample composition sensitivity). We require all archetypes to clear a mean Jaccard overlap floor of $\ge 0.60$ under both regimes.

The bootstrap evidence establishes three empirical conclusions (@fig-archetype-stability):

1. **$k = 3$ is robust across resampling regimes:** It is the only candidate model where every archetype clears the 0.60 reproducibility floor under both frame-level measurement error and firm-level sample composition sensitivity.
2. **Failed falsification at $k = 4$:** Partition stability breaks down globally at $k = 4$. The fourth vertex isolates ungrounded promotional rhetoric without technical specificity, anchored by only a handful of firms. Rather than an autonomous statutory posture, isolated promotional hype represents sampling noise, confirming that AI washing is better modeled as inter-channel decoupling (Chapter 5).
3. **Rejection of $k = 2$ on substantive grounds:** Although mathematically stable, collapsing to two poles eliminates governance orientation entirely, erasing the institutional distinction between board oversight and statutory risk warnings.[^k2-note]

[^k2-note]: In $k = 2$, Archetype 0 exhibits promotional $=$ `{python} f"{k2_promo[0]:+.2f}"`, risk $=$ `{python} f"{k2_risk[0]:+.2f}"`, governance $=$ `{python} f"{k2_gov[0]:+.2f}"`, specificity $=$ `{python} f"{k2_spec[0]:+.2f}"`; Archetype 1 exhibits promotional $=$ `{python} f"{k2_promo[1]:+.2f}"`, risk $=$ `{python} f"{k2_risk[1]:+.2f}"`, governance $=$ `{python} f"{k2_gov[1]:+.2f}"`, specificity $=$ `{python} f"{k2_spec[1]:+.2f}"`. A discrete K-means benchmark on the same standardized posture matrix reproduces the same three-archetype partition (kept in the project's supplementary analytics files rather than reproduced in the appendix).

A principal components diagnostic confirms that the space cannot be collapsed into one score without heavy information loss: the first two components capture `{python} f"{hd_pca_ev[0] + hd_pca_ev[1]:.1f}"`% of the variance (PC1: `{python} f"{hd_pca_ev[0]:.1f}"`%, PC2: `{python} f"{hd_pca_ev[1]:.1f}"`%).

### Theoretical interpretation: signaling and disclosure costs

Through the signaling lens [@spence1973; @verrecchia1983], corporate disclosure postures reflect differing proprietary and litigation costs. Vocal Substantives face high disclosure costs: under Rule 10b-5 anti-fraud liability, forward-looking commercial claims must be substantiated with verifiable technical investments to avoid legal exposure.

In contrast, Governance-Led Disclosers face low proprietary costs, directing communication toward board oversight charters and compliance guardrails to satisfy institutional investors [@suchman1995]. Defensive Disclosers incur the lowest disclosure costs, satisfying statutory mandates by pooling boilerplate risk warnings in Item 1A without committing management to operational milestones.

### Out-of-sample temporal validation

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
# Out-of-sample temporal validation on firm-year posture vectors: fit k-means
# (k = 3) on the training window, assign 2025 firm-years to the frozen
# centroids, and compare with an unconstrained k-means refit on 2025 alone.
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


_fy = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_year_strategy_dimensions.parquet"))
_FE = ["promotional_posture", "hedging_posture", "risk_orientation", "governance_orientation", "temporal_posture",
       "ai_positioning", "specificity", "disclosure_intensity"]
_fy = _fy[(_fy["archetype"] != "No AI") & _fy[_FE].notna().all(axis=1)]

def _kmeans(X, k=3, seed=42, n_init=10, iters=300):
    best = None
    for s in range(n_init):
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed + s)
        C = X[rng.choice(len(X), k, replace=False)]
        for _ in range(iters):
            lab = np.argmin(((X[:, None, :] - C[None]) ** 2).sum(-1), axis=1)
            C2 = np.array([X[lab == j].mean(0) if (lab == j).any() else C[j] for j in range(k)])
            if np.allclose(C, C2):
                break
            C = C2
        inertia = ((X - C[lab]) ** 2).sum()
        if best is None or inertia < best[0]:
            best = (inertia, C, lab)
    return best[1], best[2]

def _ari(a, b):
    ct = pd.crosstab(a, b).values
    comb = lambda x: x * (x - 1) / 2
    n = ct.sum(); sij = comb(ct).sum(); si = comb(ct.sum(1)).sum(); sj = comb(ct.sum(0)).sum()
    e = si * sj / comb(n)
    return (sij - e) / ((si + sj) / 2 - e)

def _oos(train_years, test_year=2025):
    tr = _fy[_fy["year"].isin(train_years)]
    te = _fy[_fy["year"] == test_year]
    mu, sd = tr[_FE].mean(), tr[_FE].std()
    Xtr = ((tr[_FE] - mu) / sd).values
    Xte = ((te[_FE] - mu) / sd).values
    C, _ = _kmeans(Xtr)
    frozen = np.argmin(((Xte[:, None, :] - C[None]) ** 2).sum(-1), axis=1)
    _, refit = _kmeans(Xte)
    lab_tr = np.argmin(((Xtr[:, None, :] - C[None]) ** 2).sum(-1), axis=1)
    names = {}
    for j in range(3):
        names[j] = tr["archetype"].values[lab_tr == j].tolist()
        names[j] = max(set(names[j]), key=names[j].count) if names[j] else f"cluster {j}"
    jac = {}
    for j in range(3):
        a = frozen == j
        jac[names[j]] = max(((a & (refit == r)).sum() / max((a | (refit == r)).sum(), 1)) for r in range(3)) * 100
    return _ari(frozen, refit), jac, len(te)

oos_ari_2124, oos_jac_2124, oos_n_2025 = _oos([2021, 2022, 2023, 2024])
oos_ari_2123, oos_jac_2123, _ = _oos([2021, 2022, 2023])
oos_ari_2125, _, oos_n_2026 = _oos([2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025], test_year=2026)
oos_jac_min, oos_jac_max = min(oos_jac_2124.values()), max(oos_jac_2124.values())
oos_vs_2123 = oos_jac_2123.get("Vocal Substantives", float("nan"))
```

The taxonomy also holds out of sample. A model frozen on the 2021–2024 firm-years is applied to the `{python} oos_n_2025` firm-years of 2025, reaching ARI = `{python} f"{oos_ari_2124:.3f}"` against an unconstrained 2025 refit with Jaccard recovery of `{python} f"{oos_jac_min:.1f}"`–`{python} f"{oos_jac_max:.1f}"`% across archetypes. Even the stricter pre-GenAI 2021–2023 training window keeps meaningful post-2023 recovery (ARI = `{python} f"{oos_ari_2123:.3f}"`; Vocal Substantives recovered at `{python} f"{oos_vs_2123:.1f}"`%).

Freezing on 2021–2025 and testing on the `{python} oos_n_2026` firm-years observed so far in 2026 gives ARI = `{python} f"{oos_ari_2125:.3f}"`. Posture rates do not depend on calendar progress, confirming that the taxonomy is not an artifact of the initial commercialization wave.

- **Technology** concentrates heavily in Vocal Substantives, as enterprise software and infrastructure providers have both the capability and the commercial incentive to market client-facing AI products.
- **Financial Services, Utilities, and Healthcare** dominate Governance-Led Disclosers, reflecting strict compliance environments where model-risk management, board oversight, and responsible AI guardrails take precedence.
- **Communications, Business Services, and Retail** lead Defensive Disclosers, framing artificial intelligence primarily as an industry disruption or operational vulnerability rather than an affirmative commercial product.
- **Energy & Mining and Manufacturing** concentrate in No AI, where operational transformation remains centered on physical assets and capital extraction rather than narrative AI claims.

This sorting aligns with institutional theory: firms facing shared regulatory scrutiny converge on matching disclosure registers [@dimaggio1983, pp. 147--48; @suchman1995, pp. 571--74]. Corporate posture is therefore substantially an industry norm rather than solely an idiosyncratic firm choice.

#### Institutional channels: where vs. how firms disclose

The empirical correlations between archetypal weights and regulatory document sources reveal that *where* a firm discloses and *how* it discloses are not separable. Across all $N =$ `{python} _ch_n_disclosing` disclosing firms, archetypal weights exhibit substantial correlations with specific statutory channels:

- **Defensive Disclosers ($w_{\text{Def}}$):** Aligns strongly ($r = +0.763, R^2 = 58.2\%$) with Form 10-K Item 1A (Risk Factors), where disclosures focus exclusively on regulatory hazards, liabilities, and vendor dependencies in the absence of promotional language.
- **Governance-Led Disclosers ($w_{\text{Gov}}$):** Aligns strongly ($r = +0.607, R^2 = 36.8\%$) with Form DEF 14A proxy statements, where communication centers on board committee charters, supervisory accountability, and executive oversight.
- **Vocal Substantives ($w_{\text{Vocal}}$):** Aligns positively ($r = +0.575, R^2 = 33.1\%$) with Form 10-K Item 1 (Business Description) and Item 7 (MD&A), which serve as the primary statutory vehicles for articulating commercial strategy and operational milestones.

These correlations confirm that the archetypes represent *postures in channel*. Statutory channel selection is a primary strategic choice [@campbell2014, pp. 396--98]: restricting AI mentions to Item 1A is an inherently defensive posture, while elevating AI to proxy statements is an active governance choice. An audit confirms `{python} _ch_n_coverage_pct`% DEF 14A filing coverage for all $N =$ `{python} _ch_n_disclosing` disclosing firms (`{python} _ch_n_mention` mention AI, `{python} _ch_n_omit` omit it), proving that low $w_{\text{Gov}}$ reflects an active corporate omission rather than missing filing data.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import os
from archetypes import AA as _AA10k

_posture_cols_10k = ["promotional_posture", "hedging_posture", "risk_orientation", "governance_orientation",
                     "temporal_posture", "ai_positioning", "specificity"]

def _posture_10k(d):
    d = d.copy()
    concepts = d["concepts"].apply(lambda c: set(c) if c is not None else set())
    d["promotional_posture"] = d["rhetoric"].apply(
        lambda r: np.mean([x in list(r) if r is not None else False for x in ("promotional", "strategic")]))
    d["hedging_posture"] = d["rhetoric"].apply(lambda r: float("hedged" in list(r)) if r is not None else 0.0)
    d["risk_orientation"] = concepts.apply(lambda s: float(any(str(c).startswith("risk_") for c in s)))
    d["governance_orientation"] = concepts.apply(lambda s: float(any(str(c).startswith("gov_") for c in s)))
    d["temporal_posture"] = (d["temporal"] == "realized").astype(float)
    d["ai_positioning"] = d["is_customer_facing"].astype(float)
    d["specificity"] = d["specificity"].apply(lambda s: len(s) / 5.0 if s is not None else 0.0)
    out = d.groupby("ticker")[_posture_cols_10k].mean()
    out["n_frames_10k"] = d.groupby("ticker").size()
    return out.reset_index()

def _shrink_10k(rates, counts):
    out = {}
    for col in rates.columns:
        p = rates[col]
        mean, var = float(p.mean()), float(p.var(ddof=1))
        if var <= 0 or not 0 < mean < 1:
            out[col] = p
            continue
        strength = max(mean * (1 - mean) / var - 1, 1e-6)
        alpha, beta = mean * strength, (1 - mean) * strength
        out[col] = (p * counts + alpha) / (counts + alpha + beta)
    return pd.DataFrame(out, index=rates.index)

_frames_10k = con.execute("""
    WITH frame_domains AS (
        SELECT text_hash, frame_id, bool_or(domain = 'customer_facing') AS is_customer_facing
        FROM gold_ai_activities WHERE has_activity GROUP BY text_hash, frame_id
    )
    SELECT fm.ticker, f.concepts, f.temporal, f.specificity, f.rhetoric,
           COALESCE(fd.is_customer_facing, false) AS is_customer_facing
    FROM gold_ai_frames f
    LEFT JOIN frame_domains fd ON fd.text_hash = f.text_hash AND fd.frame_id = f.frame_id
    JOIN filing_manifest fm USING (country_code, accession_number)
    WHERE f.country_code = 'us' AND f.has_frame AND fm.ticker IS NOT NULL AND fm.form_type = '10-K'
""").fetchdf()

_p10k = _posture_10k(_frames_10k)
_p10k = _p10k[_p10k["n_frames_10k"] >= 5].reset_index(drop=True)
_shrunk10k = _shrink_10k(_p10k[_posture_cols_10k], _p10k["n_frames_10k"])
_shrunk10k["disclosure_intensity"] = _p10k["n_frames_10k"].rank(pct=True).values
_feats10k = _posture_cols_10k + ["disclosure_intensity"]
_X10k_raw = _shrunk10k[_feats10k].values
_X10k = (_X10k_raw - _X10k_raw.mean(axis=0)) / _X10k_raw.std(axis=0, ddof=0)
_aa10k = _AA10k(n_archetypes=3, random_state=42, max_iter=500)
_W10k = _aa10k.fit_transform(_X10k)
_A10k = _aa10k.archetypes_
_def_col10k = int(np.argmax(_A10k[:, _feats10k.index("risk_orientation")]))
_rem10k = [i for i in range(3) if i != _def_col10k]
_gov_col10k = max(_rem10k, key=lambda i: _A10k[i, _feats10k.index("governance_orientation")])
_voc_col10k = [i for i in range(3) if i not in (_def_col10k, _gov_col10k)][0]

_w10k_named = pd.DataFrame({
    "Vocal": _W10k[:, _voc_col10k], "Governance": _W10k[:, _gov_col10k], "Defensive": _W10k[:, _def_col10k],
}, index=_p10k["ticker"])

_common10k = W_named.index.intersection(_w10k_named.index)
_r_vocal_10k = W_named.loc[_common10k, "Vocal"].corr(_w10k_named.loc[_common10k, "Vocal"])
_r_gov_10k = W_named.loc[_common10k, "Governance"].corr(_w10k_named.loc[_common10k, "Governance"])
_r_def_10k = W_named.loc[_common10k, "Defensive"].corr(_w10k_named.loc[_common10k, "Defensive"])
_z_gov10k_on_gov = _A10k[_gov_col10k, _feats10k.index("governance_orientation")]
_z_gov10k_on_risk = _A10k[_gov_col10k, _feats10k.index("risk_orientation")]
_z_def_full_on_risk = A[def_col, SIMPLEX_FEATS.index("risk_orientation")]
_z_def10k_on_risk = _A10k[_def_col10k, _feats10k.index("risk_orientation")]
```

Recomputing the archetypes on Form 10-K frames alone (`{python} len(_common10k)` firms with >= 5 10-K-only frames) confirms that corporate governance is, by design, a proxy-channel posture. Vocal Substantives ($r =$ `{python} f"{_r_vocal_10k:.3f}"`) and Defensive Disclosers ($r =$ `{python} f"{_r_def_10k:.3f}"`) replicate robustly, but the governance vertex reallocates ($r =$ `{python} f"{_r_gov_10k:.3f}"`, with $z_{\text{gov}} =$ `{python} f"{_z_gov10k_on_gov:+.2f}"` SD concentrated in a few regulated firms).

Without DEF 14A, the governance vertex absorbs `{python} f"{_z_gov10k_on_risk:+.2f}"` SD of risk orientation while the defensive vertex attenuates from `{python} f"{_z_def_full_on_risk:+.2f}"` to `{python} f"{_z_def10k_on_risk:+.2f}"` SD; proxy statements are essential to disentangle board oversight from statutory risk-listing.

# AI Activity, Business Models, and Economic Profiles

## What corporate AI activity actually consists of

We now test whether the four disclosure archetypes line up with disclosed AI activity, which was extracted separately. Across `{python} hd_n_activity_firms` S&P 500 firms, the extraction finds `{python} f"{hd_n_activities:,}"` unique AI activity claims. For each one it records the action, the object, the business domain, the operational stage, the evidence strength, and where the technology comes from.

To make the activities readable for managers, we group them into six business roles:

- **Operate:** AI that runs the business better, from supply chains and process automation to forecasting, logistics, and back-office finance.
- **Serve:** AI that talks to customers, such as service chatbots, client chat interfaces, recommendation engines, and targeted marketing.
- **Sell:** AI built into the products themselves, such as AI features, generative tools, and predictive analytics inside customer-facing software.
- **Enable:** AI that helps employees work, such as developer copilots, code generation, enterprise search, and internal tools.
- **Control:** AI that protects the firm, such as fraud detection, cybersecurity anomaly detection, compliance monitoring, and model risk oversight.
- **Build:** the AI plumbing, such as company data platforms, cloud infrastructure, and training the firm's own foundation models.

```{python}
#| label: fig-activity-map
#| fig-cap: "Corporate AI activity map: heatmap of disclosed AI activities across business purpose and operational action type."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9.0
#| fig-height: 4.2
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


df = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_activities.parquet"))

def get_domain(row):
    f = str(row["function_family"])
    obj = str(row["object_family"])
    tgt = str(row["target"])
    if f in ["product_feature", "content_and_media"] or "product" in obj or tgt == "customers":
        return "Customer products & services (Sell)"
    elif f in ["customer_service", "marketing_and_sales"]:
        return "Sales, marketing & service (Serve)"
    elif f in ["software_development", "hr_and_talent"] or "copilot" in obj or "talent" in obj:
        return "Employee productivity & software (Enable)"
    elif f in ["it_and_cybersecurity", "fraud_and_risk", "governance"] or "security" in obj or "governance" in obj:
        return "Risk, security & governance (Control)"
    elif f in ["ai_compute_and_models", "research_and_product_development", "data_and_analytics"] or "compute" in obj or "analytics" in obj:
        return "Data, compute & models (Build)"
    else:
        return "Internal operations & workflows (Operate)"

def get_action(row):
    a = str(row["action"])
    obj = str(row["object_family"])
    stage = str(row["stage"])
    # `pilot_or_explore` (v1 action) has no v2 equivalent: piloting/exploring
    # is now a `stage`, not an action of its own (docs/migration_v1_to_v2_
    # analytics.md §1.2) -- checked first so it still reads as its own
    # bucket on this map, same as it did as a standalone v1 action.
    if stage in ("exploring", "piloting"):
        return "Pilot / Explore"
    if a in ["deploy", "scale", "integrate"]:
        if "automation" in obj:
            return "Automate"
        return "Deploy / Integrate"
    elif a in ["develop", "invest"]:
        return "Develop / Build"
    elif a in ["partner", "procure"]:
        return "Partner / Buy"
    elif a in ["measure"]:
        return "Analyze / Measure"
    elif a in ["govern", "restrict"]:
        return "Govern / Control"
    return "Deploy / Integrate"

df["domain_clean"] = df.apply(get_domain, axis=1)
df["action_clean"] = df.apply(get_action, axis=1)

rows_order = [
    "Customer products & services (Sell)",
    "Internal operations & workflows (Operate)",
    "Data, compute & models (Build)",
    "Employee productivity & software (Enable)",
    "Risk, security & governance (Control)",
    "Sales, marketing & service (Serve)"
]
cols_order = [
    "Deploy / Integrate",
    "Develop / Build",
    "Partner / Buy",
    "Pilot / Explore",
    "Analyze / Measure",
    "Automate",
    "Govern / Control"
]

ct_raw = pd.crosstab(df["domain_clean"], df["action_clean"]).reindex(index=rows_order, columns=cols_order).fillna(0)
row_pct = ct_raw.div(ct_raw.sum(axis=1), axis=0) * 100
total_acts = ct_raw.values.sum()

row_labels = [
    f"{r}\n[n = {int(ct_raw.loc[r].sum()):,}; {ct_raw.loc[r].sum()/total_acts*100:.1f}% AI acts]"
    for r in rows_order
]
col_labels = [
    f"{c}\n[n = {int(ct_raw[c].sum()):,}; {ct_raw[c].sum()/total_acts*100:.1f}% AI acts]"
    for c in cols_order
]

row_norm = row_pct.div(row_pct.max(axis=1), axis=0).values

cmap = plt.cm.Blues
rgba = cmap(row_norm)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.8, 4.8), dpi=300)
im = ax.imshow(rgba, aspect="auto")

ax.set_xticks(range(len(cols_order)))
ax.set_xticklabels(col_labels, fontsize=8.0, fontweight="bold", rotation=25, ha="right", rotation_mode="anchor")
ax.set_yticks(range(len(rows_order)))
ax.set_yticklabels(row_labels, fontsize=8.0, fontweight="bold")

for i in range(len(rows_order)):
    for j in range(len(cols_order)):
        val = int(ct_raw.iloc[i, j])
        r_pct = row_pct.iloc[i, j]
        intensity = row_norm[i, j]
        text_color = "white" if intensity >= 0.55 else "#0F172A"
        ax.text(j, i, f"{val:,}\n({r_pct:.1f}%)", ha="center", va="center",
                color=text_color, fontsize=7.8, fontweight="bold" if intensity > 0.3 else "normal")

sm = plt.cm.ScalarMappable(cmap=cmap, norm=plt.Normalize(vmin=0, vmax=100))
cbar = fig.colorbar(sm, ax=ax, fraction=0.03, pad=0.04)
cbar.set_ticks([0, 25, 50, 75, 100])
cbar.set_ticklabels(["0%", "25%", "50%", "75%", "Row max"])
cbar.ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
cbar.set_label("Within-row intensity (% of row maximum)", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold")

ax.set_title(f"Corporate AI Activity Map: Business Purpose × Action Type (n = {int(total_acts):,} AI activities)\n[Cells report counts and row percentages; shading normalized row-by-row]",
             fontsize=9.5, fontweight="bold", pad=12)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Corporate AI is mostly an application-layer story (@fig-activity-map). S&P 500 firms describe deploying and integrating commercial AI tools into the products and workflows they already have. Developing foundation models or building core computing infrastructure is a tiny share of total activity.

## How AI applications differ across industries

The six-role breakdown above pools every sector together. @tbl-4-sic-role-mix splits it by two-digit SIC industry (top 8 by firm count) to ask which roles are universal, present everywhere in roughly the same share, and which are concentrated in specific industries.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-4-sic-role-mix
#| tbl-cap: "Composition of disclosed AI activities by role and sector (2-digit SIC, top 8 by firm count), % of each sector's activities."
#| echo: false
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown


m4 = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_year_master_v2.parquet")).dropna(subset=["sic2"])
m4["sic2"] = m4["sic2"].astype(int).astype(str)
sic4_by_ticker = m4.groupby("ticker")["sic2"].agg(lambda s: s.mode().iloc[0])
top_sic4 = m4.groupby("sic2")["ticker"].nunique().sort_values(ascending=False).head(8).index
n_firms_sic4 = m4[m4["sic2"].isin(top_sic4)].groupby("sic2")["ticker"].nunique()

act4 = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_activities.parquet"))
act4["sic2"] = act4["ticker"].map(sic4_by_ticker)
act4 = act4[act4["sic2"].isin(top_sic4)].copy()

def _get_role4(row):
    f = str(row["function_family"]); obj = str(row["object_family"]); tgt = str(row["target"])
    if f in ["product_feature", "content_and_media"] or "product" in obj or tgt == "customers":
        return "Sell"
    elif f in ["customer_service", "marketing_and_sales"]:
        return "Serve"
    elif f in ["software_development", "hr_and_talent"] or "copilot" in obj or "talent" in obj:
        return "Enable"
    elif f in ["it_and_cybersecurity", "fraud_and_risk", "governance"] or "security" in obj or "governance" in obj:
        return "Control"
    elif f in ["ai_compute_and_models", "research_and_product_development", "data_and_analytics"] or "compute" in obj or "analytics" in obj:
        return "Build"
    else:
        return "Operate"

act4["role"] = act4.apply(_get_role4, axis=1)
ROLES4 = ["Sell", "Operate", "Build", "Enable", "Control", "Serve"]
mix4 = (pd.crosstab(act4["sic2"], act4["role"], normalize="index") * 100).reindex(top_sic4)[ROLES4]
role_range = (mix4.max() - mix4.min()).round(1)

SIC4_LABELS = {
    "73": "Business services", "38": "Instruments", "28": "Chemicals", "49": "Electric/gas/sanitary",
    "35": "Industrial/computer equip.", "67": "Holding/investment offices", "36": "Electronic equipment",
    "63": "Insurance carriers",
}
rows4 = [[SIC4_LABELS.get(s, s), int(n_firms_sic4.get(s, 0))] + [f"{mix4.loc[s, r]:.0f}%" for r in ROLES4] for s in top_sic4]
Markdown(tabulate(rows4, headers=["Sector", "Firms"] + ROLES4))
```

Sell and Operate trade off by sector and account for most of the spread: Sell ranges from `{python} f"{mix4['Sell'].min():.0f}"`% to `{python} f"{mix4['Sell'].max():.0f}"`% of a sector's activities, highest in electronic equipment and industrial/computer equipment, lowest in electric/gas/sanitary and insurance, where Operate takes up the slack instead. Build, Enable, Control, and Serve are comparatively universal: each stays within a `{python} f"{max(role_range['Build'], role_range['Enable'], role_range['Control'], role_range['Serve']):.0f}"`-point band across every sector in the table, the kind of AI activity most firms do a little of regardless of industry. Control is the partial exception, running highest in the two financial-services sectors (insurance, holding/investment offices), consistent with a regulatory-compliance function rather than a commercial one. The full breakdown across all sectors, plus the same cut by disclosure posture and grounding, is in Appendix G.

## Disclosure strategy meets disclosed AI activity

The central test links communication posture to disclosed AI activity. The activity inventory was never an input to the clustering. The archetypes come only from frame-level communication posture. Crossing the archetypes with activity features shows that posture maps directly onto operational disclosure (@fig-archetype-activity-heatmap and @tbl-4-1-archetype-profile):

```{python}
#| label: fig-archetype-activity-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Disclosed AI activity profile across communication archetypes. Cell values report raw activity rates; shading indicates standardized intensity across archetypes."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8.0
#| fig-height: 3.8
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


df_strat = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_strategy_dimensions.parquet"))
act = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_activities.parquet")).merge(df_strat[["ticker", "archetype"]], on="ticker", how="left")
act["archetype"] = act["archetype"].fillna("No AI")

ARCH = ["Vocal Substantives", "Governance-Led Disclosers", "Defensive Disclosers"]
n_activities = act.groupby("ticker").size()
per_firm = df_strat.set_index("ticker")["archetype"].to_frame().join(n_activities.rename("n_activities")).fillna(0)

act["proprietary_ai"] = (act["action"] == "develop") | (act["source"] == "own")
act["own_brand_named"] = act["own_brands"].map(lambda v: len(v) > 0)
act["quantified_outcome"] = (act["action"] == "measure") | (act["evidence_type"] == "metric")
act["deployed_or_scaled"] = act["stage"].isin(["deployed", "scaled"])
act["customer_target"] = act["target"] == "customers"

act_features = [
    ("Median AI activities / firm", [per_firm[per_firm.archetype == a]["n_activities"].median() for a in ARCH]),
    ("Proprietary AI share (%)", [act[act.archetype == a]["proprietary_ai"].mean() * 100 for a in ARCH]),
    ("Own brand named (%)", [act[act.archetype == a]["own_brand_named"].mean() * 100 for a in ARCH]),
    ("Customer-facing share (%)", [act[act.archetype == a]["customer_target"].mean() * 100 for a in ARCH]),
    ("Deployed / scaled (%)", [act[act.archetype == a]["deployed_or_scaled"].mean() * 100 for a in ARCH]),
    ("Quantified metric (%)", [act[act.archetype == a]["quantified_outcome"].mean() * 100 for a in ARCH])
]

mat_act = np.array([vals for _, vals in act_features])
mat_act_z = (mat_act - mat_act.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)) / (mat_act.std(axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.2), dpi=300)
vmax = float(np.abs(mat_act_z).max())
im = ax.imshow(mat_act_z, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-vmax, vmax=vmax, aspect="auto")

ax.set_xticks(range(3))
ax.set_xticklabels(ARCH, fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold", rotation=30, ha="right", rotation_mode="anchor")
ax.set_yticks(range(len(act_features)))
ax.set_yticklabels([name for name, _ in act_features], fontsize=8.8, fontweight="bold")

for i in range(len(act_features)):
    for j in range(3):
        raw_v = mat_act[i, j]
        z_v = mat_act_z[i, j]
        fmt_val = f"{raw_v:.0f}" if i == 0 else f"{raw_v:.1f}%"
        ax.text(j, i, fmt_val, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold",
                color="white" if abs(z_v) > vmax * 0.55 else "#0F172A")

cbar = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.85, pad=0.03)
cbar.set_label("Standardized difference (z-score)", fontsize=8.0)
ax.set_title("Disclosed AI Activity Profile Across Communication Archetypes",
             fontsize=9.8, fontweight="bold", pad=12)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-4-1-archetype-profile
#| tbl-cap: "Disclosed AI activity profile by disclosure archetype, from the disclosed AI activity inventory (never an input to the posture clustering)."
#| echo: false
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown


strat = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_strategy_dimensions.parquet"))[["ticker", "archetype"]]
act = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_activities.parquet")).merge(strat, on="ticker", how="left")

def share(col):
    return [f"{act[act.archetype == a][col].mean() * 100:.1f}%" for a in ARCH]

act["proprietary_ai"] = (act["action"] == "develop") | (act["source"] == "own")
act["own_brand_named"] = act["own_brands"].map(lambda v: len(v) > 0)
```
