```{python}
act["customer_target"] = act["target"] == "customers"

rows = [
    ["Disclosed AI activities per firm (median)"] + [f"{per_firm[per_firm.archetype == a]['n_activities'].median():.0f}" for a in ARCH],
    ["Customer-facing AI activity share (%)"] + share("customer_target"),
    ["Technology source: proprietary/own (%)"] + share("proprietary_ai"),
    ["AI activities naming an own product/brand (%)"] + share("own_brand_named"),
    ["AI activities reporting a quantified outcome (%)"] + share("quantified_outcome"),
    ["AI activities at stage deployed/scaled (%)"] + share("deployed_or_scaled"),
]
headers = ["AI activity feature"] + [f"{a} (n={n_firms[a]})" for a in ARCH]
Markdown(tabulate(rows, headers=headers))
```

*Notes:* Figures computed from the `{python} f"{hd_n_activities:,}"`-AI-activity inventory (`{python} hd_n_activity_firms` firms with at least one disclosed AI activity out of the `{python} hd_n_universe`-firm universe). The inventory is joined after the fact to the posture-based archetype assignment. Column headers give the number of firms per archetype in the full universe, so firms without any activity count as zeros. "No AI" firms with positive activity counts reflect earnings-call statements by firms whose formal SEC filings omit AI entirely. The full 14-variable AI activity profile (of which this table shows the 6 headline variables) is kept in the project's supplementary analytics files.

Vocal Substantives lead on every measure of operational depth: more AI activities, more proprietary technology, more customer-facing deployment, and more production-stage systems. Governance-Led Disclosers sit in the middle. Defensive Disclosers report the thinnest and least mature inventory.

Frames and activities come from the same corporate text, so the activity gap could simply reflect that some firms write more. To rule this out, we regress disclosed AI activity counts on the archetypes and control for total AI disclosure volume ($\log(1 + \text{AI frames})$). The model is a negative binomial regression:

$$
\log \mathbb{E}[\text{AI Activities}_i] = \alpha + \beta_1 \text{VocalSubstantives}_i + \beta_2 \text{GovernanceLed}_i + \gamma \log(1 + \text{Frames}_i)
$$

```{python}
#| label: tbl-4-1b-volume-adjusted
#| tbl-cap: "Disclosed AI activity count by archetype, before and after conditioning on total AI disclosure volume (log frame count). Reference category: Defensive Disclosers."
#| echo: false
import json
from pathlib import Path
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown


reg = json.loads(_p("strategy_dimensions_manifest.json").read_text())["activity_volume_regression"]
OTHERS = ["Governance-Led Disclosers", "Vocal Substantives"]

def fmt_p(p):
    return "<0.001" if p < 0.001 else f"{p:.3f}"

rows = [[a, f"{reg['raw'][a]['ratio']:.2f}x", fmt_p(reg['raw'][a]['p']),
        f"{reg['volume_adjusted'][a]['ratio']:.2f}x", fmt_p(reg['volume_adjusted'][a]['p'])] for a in OTHERS]
rows.append(["log(1 + AI frames)", "-", "-", f"{reg['log_frames_coef']:+.2f} (coef.)", fmt_p(reg['log_frames_p'])])
Markdown(tabulate(rows, headers=[f"Archetype vs. {reg['reference']}", "Raw ratio", "p", "Volume-adjusted ratio", "p"]))
```

A real difference survives the volume control. At the same total disclosure volume, Vocal Substantives still report `{python} f"{hd_vs_ratio:.2f}"` times as many AI activities as Defensive Disclosers ($p < 0.001$). Governance-Led Disclosers report `{python} f"{hd_gl_ratio:.2f}"` times as many ($p < 0.001$). Volume does explain most of the raw gap, as the shared-source concern predicts. Log frame count alone gives a pseudo-$R^2$ of `{python} f"{hd_vol_r2:.2f}"` in the adjusted model. Posture is not just wordiness; it reflects different amounts of disclosed AI activity.

## What firms actually do differently

The archetypes differ not only in how many activities they disclose but in what those activities are for (@fig-archetype-activity-mix):

```{python}
#| label: fig-archetype-activity-mix
#| fig-cap: "Mix of disclosed corporate AI activities by disclosure archetype (100% stacked horizontal bars). Vocal Substantives dedicate over 60% of AI activities to client products (Sell); Governance-Led prioritize internal operations (Operate) and governance control (Control)."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9.2
#| fig-height: 3.6
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


df_strat = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_strategy_dimensions.parquet"))
act = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_activities.parquet")).merge(df_strat[["ticker", "archetype"]], on="ticker", how="left")
act["archetype"] = act["archetype"].fillna("No AI")

def get_role(row):
    f = str(row["function_family"])
    obj = str(row["object_family"])
    tgt = str(row["target"])
    if f in ["product_feature", "content_and_media"] or "product" in obj or tgt == "customers":
        return "Sell (Customer products)"
    elif f in ["customer_service", "marketing_and_sales"]:
        return "Serve (Sales & service)"
    elif f in ["software_development", "hr_and_talent"] or "copilot" in obj or "talent" in obj:
        return "Enable (Productivity & dev)"
    elif f in ["it_and_cybersecurity", "fraud_and_risk", "governance"] or "security" in obj or "governance" in obj:
        return "Control (Risk & security)"
    elif f in ["ai_compute_and_models", "research_and_product_development", "data_and_analytics"] or "compute" in obj or "analytics" in obj:
        return "Build (Compute & data)"
    else:
        return "Operate (Internal operations)"

act["role"] = act.apply(get_role, axis=1)
ARCH = ["Vocal Substantives", "Governance-Led Disclosers", "Defensive Disclosers"]
ct_mix = pd.crosstab(act["archetype"], act["role"], normalize="index") * 100

roles_order = [
    "Sell (Customer products)",
    "Operate (Internal operations)",
    "Build (Compute & data)",
    "Enable (Productivity & dev)",
    "Control (Risk & security)",
    "Serve (Sales & service)"
]
colors = ["#1D4ED8", "#0D9488", "#D97706", "#6366F1", "#DC2626", "#E11D48"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.2, 3.6), dpi=300)
y_pos = np.arange(3)
left = np.zeros(3)

for role, col in zip(roles_order, colors):
    vals = [ct_mix.loc[a, role] for a in ARCH]
    bars = ax.barh(y_pos, vals, left=left, color=col, edgecolor="white", height=0.55, label=role)
    for idx, (b, v) in enumerate(zip(bars, vals)):
        if v >= 6.0:
            ax.text(left[idx] + v/2, b.get_y() + b.get_height()/2, f"{v:.1f}%",
                    ha="center", va="center", color="white", fontsize=7.8, fontweight="bold")
    left += vals

ax.set_yticks(y_pos)
ax.set_yticklabels(ARCH, fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold")
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
ax.set_xlabel("% of Disclosed AI Activities", fontsize=8.8, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_title("Mix of Disclosed Corporate AI Activities by Disclosure Archetype (100% Stacked)",
             fontsize=10.0, fontweight="bold", pad=12)
ax.legend(bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.22), loc="upper center", ncol=3, fontsize=8.0, frameon=False)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The stacked mix in @fig-archetype-activity-mix shows where AI enters each type of firm:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
def _mix(a, role):
    return f"{ct_mix.loc[a, role]:.1f}"
_SELL, _OPER, _CTRL, _SERVE = "Sell (Customer products)", "Operate (Internal operations)", "Control (Risk & security)", "Serve (Sales & service)"
```

Vocal Substantives concentrate most heavily in Sell; Governance-Led Disclosers split closer to evenly between Sell and Operate, with Control activities a small share even here: governance is how this group talks, not mainly what it does. Defensive Disclosers describe the same commercial and operational mix as everyone else, just less of it. Sell dominates in all three groups: the archetypes differ in how strongly (Vocal Substantives most of all) and in how much they disclose, not in what corporate AI is for.

Three filings illustrate what that split looks like in practice (@tbl-archetype-activity-examples).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-archetype-activity-examples
#| tbl-cap: "Illustrative statutory filing excerpts across disclosure archetypes and activity orientations."
#| echo: false
import re
from pathlib import Path
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown

def _quote(ticker, act_df, **filters):
    sub = act_df[act_df["ticker"] == ticker]
    for k, v in filters.items():
        sub = sub[sub[k] == v]
    r = sub.iloc[0]
    q = get_db().execute("SELECT paragraph_text FROM paragraphs WHERE accession_number = ? AND paragraph_index = ? LIMIT 1",
                         [r["accession_number"], int(r["paragraph_index"])]).fetchone()
    if not q:
        return ""
    t = re.sub(r"[\x00-\x08\x0b\x0c\x0e-\x1f]", "", q[0])
    t = re.sub(r"\(see page[s]?\s*[^)]*\)", "", t)  # drop cross-page reference placeholders lost in text extraction
    t = re.sub(r"\s{2,}", " ", t)
    return re.sub(r"\s+([.,;:])", r"\1", t).strip()

def _clip(text, n=190):
    return f'"{text[:n].strip()}..."' if len(text) > n else f'"{text}"'

_amd_quote = _quote("AMD", act, role="Sell (Customer products)", evidence_type="metric")
_aig_quote = _quote("AIG", act, role="Control (Risk & security)", evidence_type="named")
_lly_quote = _quote("LLY", act, evidence_type="generic")

_rows_ex = [
    [
        "**Vocal Substantives**",
        "**AMD**",
        "Sell",
        _clip(_amd_quote, 180).replace("|", "-"),
        "Specific and verifiable: names the acquisition, product line, and deployment targets.",
    ],
    [
        "**Governance-Led Disclosers**",
        "**AIG**",
        "Control",
        _clip(_aig_quote, 180).replace("|", "-"),
        "Institutional oversight language rather than technical or operational deployment.",
    ],
    [
        "**Defensive Disclosers**",
        "**Eli Lilly**",
        "Generic (Sell / Operate)",
        _clip(_lly_quote, 180).replace("|", "-"),
        "Vague and defensive: no named products, operational stages, or concrete metrics.",
    ],
]
Markdown(tabulate(_rows_ex, headers=["Archetype", "Firm", "Primary Focus", "Filing Excerpt", "Diagnostic Interpretation"]))
```

## Decomposing AI activity grounding

Firms disclose thousands of AI activities, but the question that matters is how concretely each one is grounded in the text. To measure AI activity grounding ($G$), we pass every disclosed activity through a ladder of ever stricter requirements:

$$\text{AI Activity Claim} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Specific Business Function} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Deployed Stage} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Named Product/Process} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{Quantified Outcome Metric}$$

```{python}
#| label: fig-ladder-substance
#| fig-cap: "Decomposing AI activity grounding: cumulative nested progression of evidence requirements (left) and independent grounding attribute frequencies (right) across all disclosed AI activities."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 3.8
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

data_path = Path("../data/processed/clusters/firm_activities.parquet")
if not data_path.exists():
    data_path = Path("data/processed/clusters/firm_activities.parquet")

df = pd.read_parquet(data_path)
n_total = len(df)

# Nested counts
c1 = n_total
c2 = len(df[df["function_family"] != "unspecified"])
c3 = len(df[(df["function_family"] != "unspecified") & df["stage"].isin(["deployed", "scaled"])])
c4 = len(df[(df["function_family"] != "unspecified") & df["stage"].isin(["deployed", "scaled"]) & df["evidence_type"].isin(["named", "metric"])])
c5 = len(df[(df["function_family"] != "unspecified") & df["stage"].isin(["deployed", "scaled"]) & (df["evidence_type"] == "metric")])

pcts_nested = [c / n_total * 100 for c in [c1, c2, c3, c4, c5]]

# Independent component rates
p_func = (df["function_family"] != "unspecified").mean() * 100
p_stage = df["stage"].isin(["deployed", "scaled"]).mean() * 100
p_named = df["evidence_type"].isin(["named", "metric"]).mean() * 100
p_metric = (df["evidence_type"] == "metric").mean() * 100
p_vendor = (df["source"] == "third_party").mean() * 100

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 3.8), dpi=300)

labels_nested = [
    "1. Discloses an AI activity claim",
    "2. + Specific business function",
    "3. + Deployed / scaled stage",
    "4. + Named product or process",
    "5. + Quantified outcome / metric"
]
colors_nested = ["#94A3B8", "#64748B", "#3B82F6", "#2563EB", "#1D4ED8"]
bars1 = ax1.barh(labels_nested[::-1], pcts_nested[::-1], color=colors_nested[::-1], height=0.6)
for b, p in zip(bars1, pcts_nested[::-1]):
    ax1.text(p + 1.5, b.get_y() + b.get_height() / 2, f"{p:.1f}%", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold", color="#1E293B")
ax1.set_xlim(0, 115)
ax1.set_xlabel(f"% of all {n_total:,} disclosed AI activities", fontsize=8.8, fontweight="bold")
ax1.set_title("Decomposing AI Activity Grounding\n(Strictly Nested Concreteness Requirements)", fontsize=9.8, fontweight="bold")
ax1.grid(True, axis="x", linestyle="--", alpha=0.3)
ax1.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

labels_ind = [
    "Deployed or scaled stage",
    "Specific business function",
    "Named product or process",
    "Quantified outcome metric",
    "External vendor / model attributed"
]
pcts_ind = [p_stage, p_func, p_named, p_metric, p_vendor]
colors_ind = ["#059669", "#0284C7", "#6366F1", "#D97706", "#DC2626"]
bars2 = ax2.barh(labels_ind[::-1], pcts_ind[::-1], color=colors_ind[::-1], height=0.6)
for b, p in zip(bars2, pcts_ind[::-1]):
    ax2.text(p + 1.5, b.get_y() + b.get_height() / 2, f"{p:.1f}%", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold", color="#1E293B")
ax2.set_xlim(0, 115)
ax2.set_xlabel("% of AI activities with attribute present", fontsize=8.8, fontweight="bold")
ax2.set_title("Independent AI Grounding Attributes\n(% of AI activities meeting each criterion)", fontsize=9.8, fontweight="bold")
ax2.grid(True, axis="x", linestyle="--", alpha=0.3)
ax2.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Only `{python} f"{c5 / c1 * 100:.1f}"`% of disclosed AI activities reach the top of the ladder, pairing an operational deployment with a quantified performance metric (@fig-ladder-substance). The drop is steep: `{python} f"{c2 / c1 * 100:.1f}"`% name a business function, and `{python} f"{c3 / c1 * 100:.1f}"`% are both function-specific and deployed or scaled.

The share that also names a concrete product, process, or metric falls to `{python} f"{c4 / c1 * 100:.1f}"`%. Most disclosed AI activities are hard to judge from outside because they come with no quantified outcome.

## The paradox of the GenAI boom

The generative-AI boom multiplied the volume of disclosed AI activity and lowered its average grounding. Between 2021 and 2026 the number of disclosed activities per year rose several-fold. Over the same period three grounding shares fell (@fig-volume-vs-grounding). Fewer activities were at a deployed or scaled stage, fewer named a specific product or process, and fewer had an identified business function. The activities added after 2023 are, on average, less concrete than what firms were already disclosing.

This is what institutional-legitimacy theory predicts. Once a vocabulary becomes an institutional expectation, the language spreads faster than the grounded activity behind it [@meyer1977, pp. 340--41]. Activity counts build up over the year. So the 2026 volume is shown both as observed year to date and as a full-year estimate using the same-window seasonal factor. The 2026 grounding shares are rates, so we read them as observed.

```{python}
#| label: fig-volume-vs-grounding
#| fig-cap: "The paradox of the GenAI boom: disclosed AI activity volume surged several-fold (Panel A), while marginal concreteness and grounding indicators deteriorated (Panel B), 2021–2025 (2026 shown as year-to-date)."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9.8
#| fig-height: 4.0
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

act = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_activities.parquet"))
filings = con.execute("""
    WITH manifest AS (
        SELECT country_code, accession_number, filing_date FROM filing_manifest WHERE form_type != 'Earnings call transcript'
        UNION ALL
        SELECT country_code, accession_number, filing_date FROM filing_manifest_10q
    )
    SELECT accession_number, filing_date FROM manifest
""").df()

act_f = act[act.channel == "filing"].merge(filings, on="accession_number", how="left")
act_f["year"] = pd.to_datetime(act_f["filing_date"]).dt.year
act_c = act[act.channel == "call"].copy()
act_c["year"] = act_c["accession_number"].str.extract(r"_(\d{4})Q")[0].astype(float)
both = pd.concat([act_f, act_c], ignore_index=True)
both = both[both["year"].between(2021, 2026)]
both["year"] = both["year"].astype(int)

vol = both.groupby("year").size()
dep_share = both.groupby("year")["stage"].apply(lambda s: s.isin(["deployed", "scaled"]).mean() * 100)
gen_ev = both.groupby("year")["evidence_type"].apply(lambda s: (s == "generic").mean() * 100)
named_prod = both.groupby("year")["evidence_type"].apply(lambda s: (s == "named").mean() * 100)
ident_func = both.groupby("year")["function_family"].apply(lambda s: (s != "unspecified").mean() * 100)

# Full-year 2026 projection with the same-window seasonal factor (activities
# in full 2025 / activities in the 2025 window ending on the 2026 cut-off day),
# computed once in the header chunk as hd_act_factor.
latest_date_2026 = act_f[act_f["year"] == 2026]["filing_date"].max()
months_observed = latest_date_2026.month if pd.notnull(latest_date_2026) else 8
annual_factor = hd_act_factor
vol_2026_obs = vol[2026]
vol_2026_proj_total = int(round(vol_2026_obs * annual_factor))
vol_2026_proj_adj = vol_2026_proj_total - vol_2026_obs

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.0, 4.2), dpi=300)

years = sorted(vol.index.tolist())
main_years = [y for y in years if y <= 2025]
ytd_years = [y for y in years if y >= 2025]

# Panel A: Total Disclosed Corporate AI Activities with Stacked Year-End Projection
bars_hist = ax1.bar(main_years, [vol[y] for y in main_years], color="#2563EB", width=0.55, edgecolor="#1D4ED8", lw=1.2, label="Observed full-year AI activities")
bar_26_obs = ax1.bar([2026], [vol_2026_obs], color="#60A5FA", width=0.55, edgecolor="#2563EB", lw=1.2, label="2026 YTD observed AI activities")
bar_26_proj = ax1.bar([2026], [vol_2026_proj_adj], bottom=[vol_2026_obs], color="#DBEAFE", width=0.55,
                      edgecolor="#1D4ED8", lw=1.2, linestyle="--", hatch="///", label="Projected year-end AI activity adjustment")

max_v = max(max(vol[y] for y in main_years), vol_2026_proj_total)
ax1.set_ylim(0, max_v * 1.20)

for y in main_years:
    v = vol[y]
    ax1.text(y, v + max_v * 0.02, f"{v:,}", ha="center", fontsize=8.2, fontweight="bold", color="#1E293B")

ax1.text(2026, vol_2026_obs * 0.55, f"{vol_2026_obs:,}\n(YTD)", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.8, fontweight="bold", color="#1E3A8A")
ax1.text(2026, vol_2026_proj_total + max_v * 0.02, f"{vol_2026_proj_total:,}\n(FY Proj.)", ha="center", fontsize=8.0, fontweight="bold", color="#1D4ED8")

ax1.set_ylabel("Number of Disclosed AI Activities", fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold")
ax1.set_xlabel("Year", fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold")
ax1.set_xticks(years)
ax1.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7.2, framealpha=0.9)
growth_ratio = vol[2025] / vol[2021]
proj_ratio = vol_2026_proj_total / vol[2021]
ax1.set_title(f"Panel A: AI Activity Volume Surges ({growth_ratio:.1f}× panel, {proj_ratio:.1f}× proj.)\nTotal Disclosed Corporate AI Activities", fontsize=9.5, fontweight="bold")
ax1.grid(True, axis="y", linestyle="--", alpha=0.3)
ax1.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

# Panel B: Marginal Concreteness Weakens
def _trend_label(base, series):
    return f"{base} ({series[main_years[0]]:.0f}% → {series[main_years[-1]]:.0f}%)"

ax2.plot(main_years, [dep_share[y] for y in main_years], "o-", color="#059669", lw=2.2, ms=5, label=_trend_label("Deployed or scaled", dep_share))
ax2.plot(ytd_years, [dep_share[y] for y in ytd_years], "o:", color="#059669", lw=1.8, ms=5)
ax2.plot(main_years, [ident_func[y] for y in main_years], "s-", color="#0284C7", lw=2.2, ms=5, label=_trend_label("Identifiable business function", ident_func))
ax2.plot(ytd_years, [ident_func[y] for y in ytd_years], "s:", color="#0284C7", lw=1.8, ms=5)
ax2.plot(main_years, [named_prod[y] for y in main_years], "^-", color="#6366F1", lw=2.2, ms=5, label=_trend_label("Named product or process", named_prod))
ax2.plot(ytd_years, [named_prod[y] for y in ytd_years], "^:", color="#6366F1", lw=1.8, ms=5)
ax2.plot(main_years, [gen_ev[y] for y in main_years], "d--", color="#DC2626", lw=2.2, ms=5, label=_trend_label("Generic, unanchored evidence", gen_ev))
ax2.plot(ytd_years, [gen_ev[y] for y in ytd_years], "d:", color="#DC2626", lw=1.8, ms=5)

all_shares = pd.concat([dep_share, ident_func, named_prod, gen_ev])
min_s, max_s = all_shares.min(), all_shares.max()
s_range = max_s - min_s
ax2.set_ylim(max(0, min_s - s_range * 0.15), min(100, max_s + s_range * 0.40))
ax2.set_ylabel("Share of Disclosed AI Activities (%)", fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold")
ax2.set_xlabel("Year", fontsize=9.0, fontweight="bold")
ax2.set_xticks(years)
ax2.legend(fontsize=7.2, loc="upper right", framealpha=0.92)
ax2.set_title("Panel B: Marginal Concreteness Weakens\nGrounding and Specificity Indicators Over Time", fontsize=9.5, fontweight="bold")
ax2.grid(True, linestyle="--", alpha=0.3)
ax2.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

fig.suptitle("The Paradox of the GenAI Boom: Disclosed AI Activity Expanded Faster than Observable Grounding",
             fontsize=10.5, fontweight="bold", y=0.98)
plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 1, 0.94])
plt.show()
```

The magnitudes are large: disclosed activities in 2025, the last complete year, were `{python} f"{growth_ratio:.1f}"` times the 2021 count. The full-year 2026 estimate (seasonal factor `{python} f"{hd_act_factor:.2f}"`, the ratio of full-year to same-window activity in 2025) reaches `{python} f"{proj_ratio:.1f}"` times the 2021 count.

The marginal AI activity disclosed after ChatGPT was less concrete, less mature, and more speculative than what came before it. Over 2021–2025 the share at a deployed or scaled stage fell from `{python} f"{dep_share[main_years[0]]:.0f}"`% to `{python} f"{dep_share[main_years[-1]]:.0f}"`% (`{python} f"{dep_share[2026]:.0f}"`% in 2026 year to date). The share naming a specific product or process fell from `{python} f"{named_prod[main_years[0]]:.0f}"`% to `{python} f"{named_prod[main_years[-1]]:.0f}"`% (`{python} f"{named_prod[2026]:.0f}"`% in 2026). This is a fact about information, not about capabilities: we do not claim that firms got worse at AI.

## Who owns the AI

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np


df = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_activities.parquet"))
n_activities_total = len(df)

def check_role(entities, roles):
    if entities is None or len(entities) == 0:
        return False
    return any(e.get("role") in roles for e in entities)

own_brand_pct = df["entities"].apply(lambda l: check_role(l, ["own_brand"])).mean() * 100
ext_vendor_pct = df["entities"].apply(lambda l: check_role(l, ["provider", "model"])).mean() * 100
partner_pct = df["entities"].apply(lambda l: check_role(l, ["partner"])).mean() * 100
third_party_src = (df["source"] == "third_party").mean() * 100
any_ext_provider = df.groupby("ticker")["entities"].apply(lambda s: s.apply(lambda l: check_role(l, ["provider", "model", "partner"])).any())
ext_provider_firm_pct = 100 * any_ext_provider.mean()

_VENDOR_PATTERNS = {
    "OpenAI / Microsoft Ecosystem": r"openai|chatgpt|gpt|copilot|microsoft|azure",
    "Alphabet / Google": r"google|gemini|vertex|bard|deepmind|palm",
    "NVIDIA": r"nvidia|cuda",
    "Amazon Web Services": r"amazon|aws|bedrock|sagemaker",
}

def _vendor_firm_pct(pattern):
    import re
    def has_vendor(entities):
        if entities is None or len(entities) == 0:
            return False
        return any(e.get("role") in ("provider", "model", "partner") and re.search(pattern, str(e.get("name", "")).lower()) for e in entities)
    by_firm = df.groupby("ticker")["entities"].apply(lambda s: s.apply(has_vendor).any())
    return 100 * by_firm.mean()

vendor_pcts = {name: _vendor_firm_pct(pat) for name, pat in _VENDOR_PATTERNS.items()}
```

Investors and regulators reading AI claims also want to know where the technology comes from. Do public firms build it themselves, or buy foundation models from outside hyperscalers? Named entity roles across the `{python} f"{n_activities_total:,}"` disclosed AI activity statements show a clear imbalance in where the technology is said to come from (@fig-tech-provenance):

- `{python} f"{own_brand_pct:.1f}"`% of all disclosed AI activity statements attach the firm's own brand or in-house product name to the deployment.
- `{python} f"{ext_vendor_pct:.1f}"`% cite an external technology vendor or foundation model (and `{python} f"{partner_pct:.1f}"`% name a commercial partner).
- This is despite `{python} f"{ext_provider_firm_pct:.1f}"`% of S&P 500 firms naming at least one external technology provider, model family, or hyperscaler somewhere in their disclosures.

```{python}

]
values = [own_brand_pct, third_party_src, ext_vendor_pct, partner_pct]
colors = ["#1D4ED8", "#64748B", "#DC2626", "#EA580C"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.8, 3.2), dpi=300)

for b, v in zip(bars, values[::-1]):
    ax.text(v + 0.8, b.get_y() + b.get_height() / 2, f"{v:.1f}%", va="center", fontsize=8.8, fontweight="bold", color="#0F172A")

             fontsize=10.2, fontweight="bold")
```

When firms do name an external vendor, four hyperscalers take most of the mentions. OpenAI / Microsoft Ecosystem is cited by `{python} f"{vendor_pcts['OpenAI / Microsoft Ecosystem']:.1f}"`% of firms and Alphabet / Google by `{python} f"{vendor_pcts['Alphabet / Google']:.1f}"`%. NVIDIA is cited by `{python} f"{vendor_pcts['NVIDIA']:.1f}"`% and Amazon Web Services by `{python} f"{vendor_pcts['Amazon Web Services']:.1f}"`%. The full vendor taxonomy (@tbl-vendor-ecosystem) and the breakdown of named entities (@tbl-entity-roles) are in Appendix C. Firms put their own brands in front and name the external technology stack much less often.

### Regional orientation of AI disclosure

A related question is the regional orientation of AI disclosure. When S&P 500 firms discuss AI, which parts of the world do they talk about? This covers technology providers, but also markets, competitors, and regulators.

We measure it with a regional term taxonomy applied only inside AI-context text, that is, paragraphs that already carry an extracted AI disclosure frame. A mention is any whole-word match, inside such a paragraph, of a term mapped to a region in the taxonomy: named technology entities (foundation models, hyperscalers, chipmakers, enterprise platforms) plus literal country and nationality terms (e.g. "China," "Chinese," "Japan").

Because the scan stays inside AI paragraphs, a mention never comes from an unrelated supply-chain or tariff risk factor that happens to name a country. Regions are United States, Europe, China, and Other (the full term list is in Appendix C).

The United States is measured differently. Only named technology entities count (e.g. "OpenAI," "NVIDIA"), never the literal country name. Every U.S.-based filer names its own country all the time, and a literal match would swamp the U.S. share. Every other region is matched by both named entities and literal country/nationality terms, so the United States share reported here is, if anything, understated.


## External characterization of archetypes: fundamental financial profiles

Financial fundamentals and market prices do not come from disclosure text; they come from XBRL filings and market returns. We test whether the archetypes match economically distinct firms, first on raw medians and then after adjusting for sector and year. The adjusted model is $X = \alpha_{s,y} + \gamma \cdot \text{Archetype} + \varepsilon$, with No AI as the reference group and firm-clustered standard errors [@bertrand2004].

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import json
from pathlib import Path


_econ = json.loads(_p("strategy_economic_profiles.json").read_text())
econ_a = _econ["panel_a"]
d = _econ["panel_b"]

def _pfmt(p):
    return "< 0.001" if p < 0.001 else f"= {p:.3g}"

def _reg(key, seg):
    row = d[key][seg]
    return row["gamma"], row["se"], row["p"]

vs_mktcap_g, _, vs_mktcap_p = _reg("log_market_cap", "Vocal Substantives")
vs_rd_g, _, vs_rd_p = _reg("rd_intensity", "Vocal Substantives")
vs_gm_g, _, vs_gm_p = _reg("gross_margin", "Vocal Substantives")
vs_beta_g, _, vs_beta_p = _reg("beta", "Vocal Substantives")
vs_ps_g, _, vs_ps_p = _reg("ps_ratio", "Vocal Substantives")

gov_mktcap_g, _, gov_mktcap_p = _reg("log_market_cap", "Governance-Led Disclosers")
gov_roic_g, _, gov_roic_p = _reg("roic_minus_wacc", "Governance-Led Disclosers")
gov_ps_g, _, gov_ps_p = _reg("ps_ratio", "Governance-Led Disclosers")

def_rd_g, _, def_rd_p = _reg("rd_intensity", "Defensive Disclosers")

rd_vs, rd_gov, rd_def = econ_a["Vocal Substantives"]["rd_intensity"], econ_a["Governance-Led Disclosers"]["rd_intensity"], econ_a["Defensive Disclosers"]["rd_intensity"]
gm_vs, gm_gov, gm_def = econ_a["Vocal Substantives"]["gross_margin"], econ_a["Governance-Led Disclosers"]["gross_margin"], econ_a["Defensive Disclosers"]["gross_margin"]
beta_vs, beta_gov, beta_def = econ_a["Vocal Substantives"]["beta"], econ_a["Governance-Led Disclosers"]["beta"], econ_a["Defensive Disclosers"]["beta"]
```

Raw medians already put Vocal Substantives ahead of the other two archetypes on the measures that matter for a technology-heavy group: R&D/sales, gross margin, and beta. The sector-year-adjusted panel in @fig-economic-coefficients confirms this for each archetype. **Vocal Substantives** is the archetype that stands out most consistently, carrying a market-cap premium alongside higher R&D-to-sales, gross margin, beta, and price-to-sales (`{python} f"{vs_mktcap_g:+.2f}"` log points of market cap, $p$ `{python} _pfmt(vs_mktcap_p)`).

**Governance-Led Disclosers** differ from No AI mainly on scale and earnings quality, not technology intensity: a market-cap and ROIC-minus-WACC premium but little price-to-sales effect, fitting an archetype whose governance-heavy disclosure tracks firm size and regulatory exposure rather than distinctive AI economics. **Defensive Disclosers** differ least from No AI, with an R&D effect the only measure that stands out.

After sector-year adjustment, the archetype most grounded in disclosed AI activity (Vocal Substantives, @tbl-4-1-archetype-profile) is also the one that stands out most consistently on fundamentals. Talking about AI, or stressing governance, is not by itself tied to distinctive economics. This is what signalling theory predicts [@spence1973, pp. 363--64]. The information markets care about sits in the costly, specific content of disclosure, not in its volume or tone.

```{python}
#| label: fig-economic-coefficients
#| fig-cap: "Sector-year-adjusted effect of disclosure archetype on firm fundamentals, relative to No AI (95% CI, firm-clustered SE). Vocal Substantives separates most consistently from the sector-year baseline."
```

### A same-sector pair: posture, activity, and economics together

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd


_m26 = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_year_master_v2.parquet"))
_m26 = _m26[_m26["year"] == _m26["year"].max()]
_wy26 = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_year_washing_score.parquet"))
_wy26 = _wy26[_wy26["year"] == _wy26["year"].max()]

pair_year = int(_m26["year"].iloc[0])
pair = {}
for t in ["MA", "TYL"]:
    row_m, row_w = _m26[_m26["ticker"] == t].iloc[0], _wy26[_wy26["ticker"] == t].iloc[0]
    pair[t] = {"archetype": row_m["archetype"], "sic2": row_m["sic2"], "d": row_m["disclosure_intensity"],
               "market_cap": row_m["market_cap"], "beta": row_m["beta"],
               "g": row_w["grounding_index"], "w": row_w["w"]}
pair_mktcap_ratio = pair["MA"]["market_cap"] / pair["TYL"]["market_cap"]
```

Two firms in the same two-digit SIC sector (73, business services) in the `{python} pair_year` filing year illustrate why posture, disclosed activity, and economics need to be read together rather than sector alone. Mastercard (`{python} pair["MA"]["archetype"]`) and Tyler Technologies (`{python} pair["TYL"]["archetype"]`) disclose AI at a similar intensity ($D =$ `{python} f"{pair['MA']['d']:.2f}"` and `{python} f"{pair['TYL']['d']:.2f}"`), but Mastercard's disclosed activity is more than twice as grounded ($G =$ `{python} f"{pair['MA']['g']:.2f}"` versus `{python} f"{pair['TYL']['g']:.2f}"`) and its decoupling runs in the opposite direction ($W =$ `{python} f"{pair['MA']['w']:+.2f}"` versus `{python} f"{pair['TYL']['w']:+.2f}"`).

The two firms also differ sharply in scale, with Mastercard's market capitalization roughly `{python} f"{pair_mktcap_ratio:.0f}"` times Tyler's, and in market beta (`{python} f"{pair['MA']['beta']:.2f}"` versus `{python} f"{pair['TYL']['beta']:.2f}"`). Same sector, same regulatory environment, similar disclosure volume: the gap sits in what each firm reports having grounded behind that volume, and it lines up with the gap in their economics. (Appendix G disaggregates this comparison, and others like it, across sectors.)

## What disclosed AI activity adds to disclosure posture

Disclosed activity carries information that posture alone does not. At equal disclosure volume, Vocal Substantives report `{python} f"{hd_vs_ratio:.2f}"` times as many AI activities as Defensive Disclosers. Archetypes do not simply proxy for verbosity. What firms report doing is similar across groups. They sell and operate with AI. Only the archetype pairing promotion with grounded activity stands out on sector-year-adjusted fundamentals. For an investor or issuer, archetype status offers a first screen. Deeper information sits in grounding attributes. These attributes feed the credibility tests that follow.

# Credibility Under Increasing Disclosure Commitment

There is no audited census of corporate AI deployment, so we define credibility by what survives as disclosure becomes more costly to commit to [@crawford1982, pp. 1431--32; @rogers2011, pp. 2155--56]. The credibility ladder in @fig-credibility-ladder orders those commitments. Its first three rungs (named artifacts, deployment stage, quantified outcomes) are the components of AI Activity Grounding and are tested jointly through Decoupling ($W$). The last two, survival of claims across venues and response to direct SEC scrutiny, each get their own design.

## Empirical credibility tests: the credibility ladder

## Where disclosure runs ahead of substance

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import json
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd


_df_w = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_year_washing_score.parquet"))
_w = _df_w["w"].dropna()
_validation = json.loads(_p("washing_score_validation.json").read_text())
n_firm_years = _validation["n_panel"]
n_firms_panel = _validation["n_firms"]
year_min, year_max = int(_df_w["year"].min()), int(_df_w["year"].max())
```

We ask whether a firm's disclosure volume keeps pace with its concrete operational substance. Volume is Disclosure Intensity ($D$: AI frames per thousand words); substance is Disclosed Substance ($S$: log activity count weighted by AI Activity Grounding). The sample is `{python} f"{n_firm_years:,}"` disclosing firm-years (`{python} n_firms_panel` S&P 500 firms, `{python} year_min`–`{python} year_max`, `{python} year_max` shown as year-to-date).

Decoupling ($W_{it}$) is the signed difference between the percentile ranks of Disclosure Intensity ($D_{it}$) and Disclosed Substance ($S_{it}$):
$$
W_{it} = \text{pct\_rank}(D_{it}) - \text{pct\_rank}(S_{it}) \in [-1, 1]
$$
By construction, $W = 0$ means talk and substance rank the same, $W > 0$ means narrative runs ahead of grounded substance ("decoupling"), and $W < 0$ means "quiet substance."

```{python}
#| label: fig-washing-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of corporate AI disclosure–substance decoupling (W). Values of W > 0 represent narrative intensity running ahead of disclosed substance; values of W < 0 denote quiet substance. The top 5% decoupled tail is highlighted in red."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.0
import json
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde


df = pd.read_parquet(_p("firm_year_washing_score.parquet"))
w = df['w'].dropna()
validation = json.loads(_p("washing_score_validation.json").read_text())
n_firm_years = validation["n_panel"]
n_firms_panel = validation["n_firms"]
persistence_rho = validation["persistence"]["spearman"]
persistence_p = validation["persistence"]["p"]
split_half_rho = validation["split_half"]["spearman"]
split_half_p = validation["split_half"]["p"]
split_half_n = validation["split_half"]["n"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.0), dpi=300)

# Histogram with bins
n_bins = 45
counts, bins, patches = ax.hist(w, bins=n_bins, density=True, alpha=0.45, color='#94A3B8', edgecolor='white', lw=0.8)

# Color the top 5% bins in red
cutoff = w.quantile(0.95)
for p, b in zip(patches, bins[:-1]):
    if b >= cutoff:
        p.set_facecolor('#DC2626')
        p.set_alpha(0.85)
        p.set_edgecolor('#7F1D1D')

# KDE curve
kde = gaussian_kde(w, bw_method=0.15)
x_grid = np.linspace(w.min() - 0.05, w.max() + 0.05, 300)
ax.plot(x_grid, kde(x_grid), color='#0F172A', lw=2.0, label='Kernel density estimate')

# Vertical line at zero
ax.axvline(0, color='#0F172A', lw=1.2, ls='--')

# Vertical line at 95th percentile
ax.axvline(cutoff, color='#DC2626', lw=1.2, ls=':')
ax.text(cutoff + 0.02, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.75, f'Top 5% decoupled tail\n(W \u2265 {cutoff:.2f})',
        fontsize=8.0, fontweight='bold', color='#991B1B')

# Directional zone headers
ax.text(-0.35, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.90, '\u2190 Substance ahead of talk\n(Quiet substance)',
        ha='center', va='center', fontsize=8.8, fontweight='bold', color='#1E40AF',
        bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.3', facecolor='#EFF6FF', edgecolor='#93C5FD', alpha=0.9))

ax.text(0.40, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.90, 'Talk ahead of substance \u2192\n(Decoupling / Washing)',
        ha='center', va='center', fontsize=8.8, fontweight='bold', color='#991B1B',
        bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.3', facecolor='#FEF2F2', edgecolor='#FCA5A5', alpha=0.9))

# Persistence note inside
stats_text = (
    'Distribution & Persistence:\n'
    f'\u2022 n = {n_firm_years:,} firm-years ({n_firms_panel} firms)\n'
    f'\u2022 YoY Spearman \u03c1 = {persistence_rho:+.3f} (p {"< 0.001" if persistence_p < 0.001 else f"= {persistence_p:.3g}"})\n'
    f'\u2022 Split-half \u03c1 = {split_half_rho:+.3f} (p {"< 0.001" if split_half_p < 0.001 else f"= {split_half_p:.3g}"})'
)
ax.text(0.04, 0.50, stats_text, transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=8.0,
        bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.35', facecolor='#F8FAFC', edgecolor='#CBD5E1', alpha=0.92))

ax.set_xlabel('Disclosure\u2013Substance Decoupling Index (W = pct_rank(Disclosure) \u2212 pct_rank(Substance))',
              fontsize=9.0, fontweight='bold')
ax.set_ylabel('Density', fontsize=9.0, fontweight='bold')
ax.set_title('Distribution of Corporate AI Disclosure\u2013Substance Decoupling (W)',
             fontsize=10.2, fontweight='bold')
ax.set_xlim(-0.75, 0.95)
ax.grid(True, linestyle=':', alpha=0.45)
ax.spines[['top', 'right']].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
persistence_p_str = "< 0.001" if persistence_p < 0.001 else f"= {persistence_p:.3g}"
split_half_p_str = "< 0.001" if split_half_p < 0.001 else f"= {split_half_p:.3g}"
persistence_n_pairs = validation["persistence"]["n_pairs"]
```

$W$ is widely dispersed across firms (@fig-washing-distribution; $\text{standard deviation} =$ `{python} f"{std_w:.2f}"`). A descriptive cut at the 95th percentile ($W \ge$ `{python} f"{cutoff:.2f}"`) flags `{python} n_tail` firm-years in the decoupled tail. These are not firms with zero AI interest. They are companies that talk about AI a lot in outward communications while disclosing almost no verifiable operational substance.

> **Persistence of the Decoupling Posture:**
>
> Decoupling persists from one year to the next. Across `{python} persistence_n_pairs` consecutive firm-year pairs, the year-over-year Spearman $\rho =$ `{python} f"{persistence_rho:+.3f}"` (p `{python} persistence_p_str`), and split-half reliability is $\rho =$ `{python} f"{split_half_rho:+.3f}"` (p `{python} split_half_p_str`, n = `{python} split_half_n`). This looks like a lasting communication posture, not annual reporting noise.

## What changes from filing to call

If decoupling is a lasting posture, what happens when the same firm discusses AI in two venues with very different legal liability?

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import json
from pathlib import Path


grounding = json.loads(_p("activity_grounding.json").read_text())
gap = grounding["channel_gap"]
gap_n_cells, gap_n_firms = gap["n_cells"], gap["n_firms"]
```

We test this with a firm × fiscal-year fixed effects design ($\alpha_{i,t}$) across `{python} gap_n_cells` balanced firm-year cells (`{python} gap_n_firms` firms) with $\ge 3$ disclosed AI activities in both channels:

$$
Y_{i,t,\text{venue}} = \alpha_{i,t} + \beta \, \mathbf{1}[\text{venue} = \text{Call}] + \varepsilon_{i,t,\text{venue}}
$$

Each cell has exactly two observations. All of the firm's earnings calls in the fiscal year are pooled into one call observation. All of its statutory SEC filings (10-K and 10-Qs) are pooled into one filing observation. Each is expressed per thousand words or as a share of that venue's activities. The estimator measures the within-firm, within-period venue-associated difference ($\text{Call}_{i,t} - \text{Filing}_{i,t}$), with standard errors clustered by firm. This sweeps out time-invariant firm unobservables, business models, and macroeconomic conditions.

It does not sweep out features of the venue itself, such as the question-and-answer format of calls or analyst prompting. The coefficient is therefore a venue difference, not a causal effect of legal liability. Because the sample requires at least three disclosed activities in both venues, it over-represents heavier AI disclosers relative to the index.

## Promotion is not the opposite of evidence

A common assumption in corporate communication research is that promotional tone and credibility move in opposite directions: heavy promotion means empty hype, and a sober tone means real operational grounding.


## Regulatory scrutiny as an external stress test

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import json
from pathlib import Path
def _pp(rel):
    p = Path(f"../{rel}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(rel)
sec_cases = json.loads(_pp("data/processed/sec_comment_letter_cases.json").read_text())
sec_n_matched = sum(1 for d in sec_cases["letters"] if d["relevance"] != "outside universe")
sec_n_direct = sec_cases["relevance_counts"].get("direct", 0)
sec_n_adjacent = sec_cases["relevance_counts"].get("adjacent", 0)
_w = sec_cases["cases"]["WELL"]
_wk = {k: i for i, k in enumerate(_w["k"])}
def _wv(m, k, who="treated"):
    v = _w[who][m][_wk[k]] if k in _wk else None
    return "n/a" if v is None else f"{v:.3f}"
def _wd(m, who="treated"):
    a, b = _w[who][m][_wk[-1]], _w[who][m][_wk[0]]
    return "n/a" if a is None or b is None else f"{b - a:+.3f}"
def _trend(m, who="treated"):
    a, b = _w[who][m][_wk[-1]], _w[who][m][_wk[0]]
    return "fell" if b < a else ("rose" if b > a else "stayed flat")
_well_same_direction = (_w["treated"]["claim_density"][_wk[0]] - _w["treated"]["claim_density"][_wk[-1]] > 0) == \
                       (_w["controls_mean"]["claim_density"][_wk[0]] - _w["controls_mean"]["claim_density"][_wk[-1]] > 0)
_a = sec_cases["cases"]["ANET"]
_ak = {k: i for i, k in enumerate(_a["k"])}
def _ad(m, who="treated"):
    a, b = _a[who][m][_ak[-1]], _a[who][m][_ak[0]]
    return "n/a" if a is None or b is None else f"{b - a:+.3f}"
```

When the regulator questions a firm's AI claims directly, does the issuer fix the specific gap, and does it change its broader disclosure posture? SEC comment letters are a documented channel through which the staff pushes firms toward more concrete disclosure [@bozanic2017], and materiality standards for AI-specific disclosure remain an open regulatory question [@strauss2025]. The first finding here is about how rare direct scrutiny is. We ran a full-text search of every SEC staff comment letter and company response filed from 2022 to 2026 for AI-related terms. We restricted it to the analysis universe and read each staff letter. The search matches the correspondence of `{python} sec_n_matched` issuers, but only `{python} sec_n_direct` letter questions a firm's own AI claims.

That letter is the Welltower letter of 2025-04-28. It contrasts a single 10-K sentence with the "industry-leading" platform claimed on the earnings call, then asks the company to describe its data science platform and the status of its AI integration.

One further letter is adjacent: Arista Networks was required to disclose revenue by customer sector, including "Cloud and AI Titans". The rest match AI terms for unrelated reasons: a segment named "HPC & AI", a climate-risk review, an activist's proxy materials. The full inventory, with what each letter actually asks, is in Appendix F (@tbl-g1-sec-letters).

Direct regulatory scrutiny of AI claims among the largest U.S. issuers is therefore not rare but singular, and that is itself informative. Through mid-2026 the SEC's stated concern with "AI washing" had produced one comment letter on AI claims to a firm in the S&P 500 of 2021.

The one direct case moves against a simple "more talk" account of scrutiny (@fig-sec-welltower; full measures for both cases in @tbl-g2-sec-cases, Appendix F). In the first annual report filed after the letter, Welltower's AI claim density `{python} _trend("claim_density")` from `{python} _wv("claim_density", -1)` to `{python} _wv("claim_density", 0)` claims per thousand words (`{python} _wd("claim_density")`), while its matched peers' claim density `{python} _trend("claim_density", "controls_mean")` over the same window (`{python} _wd("claim_density", "controls_mean")`) -- the firm's narrative moved `{python} "with" if _well_same_direction else "against"` the industry trend.

The dimension the staff asked about, realized integration, `{python} _trend("realized_density")` from `{python} _wv("realized_density", -1)` to `{python} _wv("realized_density", 0)` (`{python} _wd("realized_density")`), while peers' `{python} _trend("realized_density", "controls_mean")` (`{python} _wd("realized_density", "controls_mean")`). No quantified metric appeared in either report (`{python} _wv("quant_density", 0)` per thousand words). Decoupling narrowed sharply, from `{python} _wv("w", -1)` to `{python} _wv("w", 0)`: the firm's disclosure rank and substance rank converged rather than diverging further.

The adjacent Arista case follows the opposite pattern. Claim density rose by `{python} _ad("claim_density")` after the segment-reporting letters, alongside a `{python} _ad("claim_density", "controls_mean")` rise at peers, with no change in quantified-metric density (`{python} _ad("quant_density")`).

Two cases cannot test whether direct regulatory scrutiny prompts more empty talk, and the one letter that actually questioned a firm's own AI claims does not fit that cheap-talk account of scrutiny. After being asked to substantiate its platform claims, Welltower added less AI text, not more, and its disclosure-substance gap narrowed rather than widened.

The adjacent case, asked about segment reporting rather than AI substantiation, shows AI narrative rising alongside its peers instead. With only one directly relevant observation, and that observation pointing away from cheap talk, the data do not support a simple "more scrutiny, more empty talk" story.

## What credibility means in this thesis

Three things survive the climb up the ladder. Decoupling between narrative intensity and grounded substance is persistent (year-over-year $\rho =$ `{python} f"{hd_w_rho:.2f}"`). The cross-venue gap comes from missing evidence in statutory filings, not from a different mix of activities. And direct regulatory scrutiny of AI claims is so rare among large issuers that it amounts to a single case; in that case the response was less AI text and a narrower gap between talk and grounded activity, not the padded, still-ungrounded narrative a cheap-talk account would predict.

AI washing in this thesis therefore means an observable, persistent Decoupling ($W$) between narrative intensity and grounded operational substance, not legal proof of fraud or nonimplementation.

# Market Relevance of Disclosure Signals

Does the systematic risk the market assigns to a firm after an earnings call follow the *volume* of its AI talk or the *substance* of its disclosed activity? The outcome throughout is post-call market beta conditioned on pre-call beta. We ask whether AI disclosure carries information about how the market prices a firm's risk, not whether it earns abnormal returns. We track communication call by call across S&P 500 firms from 2021 to 2025, separating a firm's established disclosure posture from the surprise content of a given call.

## Empirical strategy and research design

The unit of observation is a firm-date earnings call event. Transcripts from the same day are aggregated, and calls with zero AI mentions stay in the sample as valid zeros. The call date anchors the timeline:

- **Historical Posture ($\text{HistD}_{i,t^{-}}, \text{HistS}_{i,t^{-}}$):** Expanding mean of disclosure intensity and substance across calls strictly prior to date $t$.
- **Call-Specific Surprise ($\text{SurpriseD}_{i,t}, \text{SurpriseS}_{i,t}$):** Current call value minus the firm's historical mean ($\text{Value}_{i,t} - \text{Hist}_{i,t^{-}}$).
- **Disclosure Intensity ($D$):** AI frames per 1,000 words.
- **Disclosed Substance ($S$):** $S = \log(1 + n_{\text{activities}}) \times G$, where activity grounding ($G$) is the proportion of activities meeting concrete verification criteria.

Pre- and post-call market betas are estimated over non-overlapping windows to avoid look-ahead bias and earnings-announcement drift:

- $\beta^{\text{pre}}_{i,t}$ over $[-252, -21]$ trading days before the call.
- $\beta^{\text{post}}_{i,t}$ over $[+21, +126]$ trading days after the call.

## Baseline econometric model

Predetermined controls ($X^{\text{pre}}_{i,t}$) are log market cap, 60-day return momentum ($\text{Return}_{60}$), and pre-call idiosyncratic volatility. Point-in-time accounting fundamentals (ROA, leverage) come from the most recent 10-K or 10-Q filed strictly before the call ($\text{filing\_date} < \text{call\_date}$), extracted from XBRL accession facts. We estimate an ANCOVA specification conditioning on pre-call beta:

$$
\beta^{\text{post}}_{i,t} = \alpha + \beta_1 \text{HistD}_{i,t^{-}} + \beta_2 \text{HistS}_{i,t^{-}} + \beta_3 \text{SurpriseD}_{i,t} + \beta_4 \text{SurpriseS}_{i,t} + \gamma \beta^{\text{pre}}_{i,t} + \delta X^{\text{pre}}_{i,t} + \alpha_{s,y} + \epsilon_{i,t},
$$

with industry-by-year fixed effects ($\alpha_{s,y} \equiv \text{SIC2} \times \text{Year}$) and standard errors clustered by firm. Continuous regressors are standardized to zero mean and unit variance. @tbl-call-beta-baseline and @fig-call-beta-baseline report the baseline estimates.


```{python}
#| label: tbl-call-beta-baseline
#| tbl-cap: "Baseline earnings-call beta regression: standardized coefficients, 95% confidence intervals clustered by firm, and p-values."
#| echo: false
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
from tabulate import tabulate
from IPython.display import Markdown

def find_path(rel):
    p = Path(f"../{rel}")
    return p if p.exists() else Path(rel)

# One baseline for the whole chapter: the full call panel, post-call window
# [+21, +126], the same estimation the robustness table and the joint tests use.
_win_all = pd.read_csv(find_path("data/processed/clusters/call_beta_robustness_windows.csv"))
base_df = _win_all[_win_all["block"] == "beta_window[post_126]"].copy()
```

```{python}
def _bp(var):
    row = base_ai.set_index("variable").loc[var]
    p_str = "< 0.001" if row["p"] < 0.001 else f"= {row['p']:.3f}"
    return row["beta_std"], row["p"], p_str

hd_b, hd_p, hd_pstr = _bp("hist_disclosure")
hs_b, hs_p, hs_pstr = _bp("hist_substance")
sd_b, sd_p, sd_pstr = _bp("surprise_disclosure")
ss_b, ss_p, ss_pstr = _bp("surprise_substance")

def _sig(p):
    return "positive and significant" if p < 0.05 else "not statistically significant"

_disc_joint = _formal["joint_disclosure_terms"]
_sub_joint = _formal["joint_substance_terms"]
_partial_r2 = _formal["partial_r2_ai_block"]
```

The baseline covers `{python} f"{int(_formal['n_calls']):,}"` calls across `{python} int(_baseline_sample['n_firms'])` firms (`{python} int(_baseline_sample['n_fe_cells'])` industry-by-year cells). The median firm has `{python} f"{_baseline_sample['median_prior_calls']:.1f}"` prior calls in the panel, so the historical averages rest on a solid base. The same sample and specification underlie every robustness column in @tbl-call-beta-paper. The accounting-control specification, which needs quarterly balance-sheet data, is estimated on the subsample where those data exist and is reported with its own sample size. Two patterns stand out:

1. **Disclosure is `{python} _sig(sd_p)` at the call-specific margin:** Historical disclosure intensity is `{python} _sig(hd_p)` ($\beta =$ `{python} f"{hd_b:.3f}"`, $p$ `{python} hd_pstr`); call-specific surprise disclosure is $\beta =$ `{python} f"{sd_b:.3f}"` ($p$ `{python} sd_pstr`). An established disclosure posture is robustly associated with subsequent systematic risk conditional on pre-call beta; the disclosure surprise of a single call is not.
2. **Substance does not:** Historical substance ($\beta =$ `{python} f"{hs_b:.3f}"`, $p$ `{python} hs_pstr`) and surprise substance ($\beta =$ `{python} f"{ss_b:.3f}"`, $p$ `{python} ss_pstr`) are indistinguishable from zero. Joint tests say the same: the disclosure block ($\text{HistD} + \text{SurpriseD}$) is significant ($F =$ `{python} f"{_disc_joint['F']:.2f}"`, $p =$ `{python} f"{_disc_joint['p']:.3f}"`; partial $R^2 =$ `{python} f"{_partial_r2:.4f}"`), while the substance block is null ($F =$ `{python} f"{_sub_joint['F']:.2f}"`, $p =$ `{python} f"{_sub_joint['p']:.3f}"`).

## Incremental information of decoupling

Decoupling ($W$) adds nothing to the beta model once its two components are already in it. Adding firm-year $W$ to the specification estimated on the `{python} f"{hd_inc_n:,}"` firm-year observations with a matched prior-year $W$ raises $R^2$ from `{python} f"{hd_inc_r2_base:.4f}"` to `{python} f"{hd_inc_r2_w:.4f}"` ($\Delta R^2 =$ `{python} f"{hd_inc_dr2:+.4f}"`; Wald $F =$ `{python} f"{hd_inc_F:.2f}"`, $p =$ `{python} f"{hd_inc_p:.3f}"`).

Decoupling remains a persistent and managerially useful diligence signal, but in this specification it carries no incremental information about systematic risk once Disclosure Intensity and Disclosed Substance are in the model. On this evidence the market responds to the level of AI talk, not to disclosed substance and not to the gap between the two.

@tbl-call-beta-paper compares the baseline ANCOVA model to several alternative specifications: accounting controls, alternative horizons, the Fama–French three-factor benchmark [@fama1993, pp. 9--10], firm fixed effects, and first-differencing. The baseline result survives accounting controls (ROA and liabilities/assets), longer post-call horizons (up to a full trading year, $[+21, +252]$), and the Fama–French three-factor benchmark. It weakens and disappears, however, under firm fixed effects and first-difference ($\Delta\beta$) models.

The link is mostly cross-sectional sorting, not a call-induced change in systematic risk: firms that talk heavily about AI carry higher market risk than peers, but quarter-to-quarter shifts in disclosure are not associated with within-firm changes in beta. Appendix E provides full diagnostics and influence tests, and also covers leverage specifications (Debt/Equity and Liabilities/Assets).

## Interpretation and limits

1. **HistDisclosure is not concentrated in a single year, but SurpriseDisclosure never reaches significance on its own:** Leave-one-year-out regressions keep $\text{HistDisclosure}$ `{python} _hd_sig_text` ($p \le$ `{python} f"{_max_p_hd:.3f}" + _hd_detail_text`). $\text{SurpriseDisclosure}$, by contrast, `{python} "reaches p < 0.05 in at least one excluded-year specification" if _any_sd_sig else "never reaches conventional significance in any single-year exclusion"`, consistent with its null in the baseline. The association between call disclosure and post-call beta runs through a firm's persistent historical posture, not through the surprise content of any one call.
2. **Pre-call beta placebo failure:** Regressing pre-call beta ($\beta^{\text{pre}}_{[-252, -21]}$) on contemporaneous call disclosure yields $\beta =$ `{python} f"{pb_disc['beta_std']:.3f}"` ($p$ `{python} _pb_disc_p`), while substance is null ($p$ `{python} _pb_sub_p`). Firms that talk heavily about AI were already high-beta before the call, which is the cross-sectional reading of the robustness table.

# From Measurement to Managerial Application

The pipeline built and tested on `{python} hd_paragraphs_m` million paragraphs of corporate text boils down to six diagnostic questions. Five follow the measurement chain ($D \to A \to G \to S \to W$). The sixth asks whether a firm tells the same story in its calls and in its filings. @tbl-managerial-framework reads each one as a managerial and investment decision.

| Core Due-Diligence Question | Construct | Managerial & Investment Decision Read |
|---|---|---|
| **1. How much are they saying?** | Disclosure Intensity ($D$) | **Narrative Exposure:** Evaluates corporate attention to AI. High $D$ signals ambition or growth positioning, but absent grounding carries high rhetorical risk. |
| **2. What do they claim to be doing?** | Disclosed AI Activity ($A$) | **Claimed Scope:** Records whether the firm reports actionable initiatives across core business functions rather than relying on abstract buzzwords. |
| **3. How concrete is the disclosure?** | AI Activity Grounding ($G$) | **Evidentiary Rigor:** Assesses grounding attributes (scaled deployment, named product/process, quantified metric, provider transparency). |
| **4. How much grounded substance is disclosed?** | Disclosed Substance ($S$) | **Effective Substantiation:** Evaluates total volume of grounded AI activity, rewarding operational depth while penalizing empty boilerplate. |
| **5. Is narrative running ahead of execution?** | Decoupling ($W$) | **Triage / Diligence Signal:** Flags firms whose narrative volume outstrips grounded operational disclosure ($W \gg 0$) or quiet executors ($W \ll 0$). |
| **6. Does the story survive across venues?** | Cross-Venue Consistency | **Evidentiary Commitment:** Checks whether oral conference-call claims, metrics, and products are formally committed to statutory 10-Ks under legal liability. |

: The AI Disclosure Credibility Framework: translating measurement constructs into managerial decisions. {#tbl-managerial-framework}

## Applying the framework: worked corporate examples

We now run the framework on contrasting firm-years from the S&P 500 (@tbl-firm-comparisons). Corporate AI communication changes fast from one reporting cycle to the next, so we look at specific firm-years rather than multi-year averages. That is where disclosure intensity, grounding and cross-venue divergence show up in real filings and real regulatory review.

```{python}
_ws["pct_s"] = _ws.groupby("year")["substance"].rank(pct=True) * 100

_act["year"] = pd.to_datetime(_act["filing_date"]).dt.year

    p = int(round(p)); suf = "th" if 10 <= p % 100 <= 20 else {1: "st", 2: "nd", 3: "rd"}.get(p % 10, "th")
    return f"{p}{suf}"

cols, rows, cv = [], {k: [] for k in ["arch", "D", "A", "G", "S", "W", "dep", "focus", "prop"]}, {}
for t, name, y in CASES:

        rows["G"].append(f"{r['grounding_index']:.3f}")

        rows["focus"].append(f"{(a['target'] == 'internal_process').mean() * 100:.1f}% internal / {(a['target'] == 'customers').mean() * 100:.1f}% customer")
        rows["prop"].append(f"{(a['source'] == 'own').mean() * 100:.1f}% proprietary")
    else:

            rows[k].append("—")

static = {
    "posture": ["Governance, internal deployment", "Legal caution, risk avoidance", "Promotional + high specificity", "Privacy, ethical governance", "Cross-venue divergence (promotional call vs. risk boilerplate in 10-K)"],

              '*"The emergence and adoption of new technologies, including AI, require us to invest resources to adapt... and present operational and competitive risks."* (10-K Item 1A)',

    "notice": ["High governance discipline masked by moderate disclosure volume; internal workflow integration prioritized over commercial hype.",
               "Risk-factor-dominated disclosure: high legal-risk orientation, low grounding, and few deployed AI activities disclosed in the 10-K; the filing tells a reader what could go wrong, not what the firm is doing.",
               "Exceptional promotional intensity backed by deep disclosed operational substance and quantified commercial traction.",
               "Disciplined narrative volume prioritizing on-device privacy governance and brand protection over speculative monetization.",
               "**The archetypal regulatory trigger:** sharp cross-venue asymmetry where oral claims on earnings calls outpaced statutory 10-K filings, drawing a formal SEC comment letter."],
}
table = [

    ["**Dominant Posture**"] + static["posture"],
    ["**Disclosure Intensity ($D$)**"] + rows["D"],
    ["**Disclosed AI Activities ($A$)**"] + rows["A"],
    ["**AI Activity Grounding ($G$)**"] + rows["G"],
    ["**Disclosed Substance ($S$)**"] + rows["S"],
    ["**Decoupling ($W$)**"] + rows["W"],
    ["**Deployed / Scaled Share**"] + rows["dep"],
```
